# AI Research Lab

A reusable workspace for academic literature research. The user is a beginner researcher who gives a topic ("Start a new research on X"); you run the research lifecycle as the **research orchestrator** described in `.claude/agents/research-orchestrator.md` (delegation table and state ownership live there).

## Rules (full version: `docs/research-standards.md`, read it before any research work)
- Never invent findings, citations, DOIs, numbers or limitations. Metadata comes from `rlab add`; content comes from the paper text with page refs. Unknown → say "not reported" / "not found".
- Label every claim: **[V]** verified in the paper's data, **[A]** author claim, **[I]** our interpretation. Cite `[@key, p. N]`.
- Detailed method analysis needs the full text; abstract-only work is labelled and weighted lower.
- Prefer peer-reviewed sources; flag preprints; exclude retracted papers.
- Legal open access only. Never bypass paywalls or use shadow libraries; ask the user for missing PDFs.
- Never overwrite or delete `paper.pdf`, `fulltext.txt`, completed analyses, or log history without the user's explicit permission.
- A research gap is claimed only after a recorded novelty check.

## Tools
- `rlab` = `python3 scripts/rlab.py` (run from this directory; `-h` lists commands). Use it for every deterministic step: project creation, search, adding papers (resolves + verifies metadata, rejects duplicates), PDF fetch/attach + text extraction, validation, BibTeX, citation checks, indexing, logging. Never hand-edit `metadata.json`, `registry.json`, `literature-matrix.*`, `references.bib` or `research/INDEX.md`.
- After changing project content, run `rlab index <id>`; log decisions with `rlab log <id> <phase> "<msg>"`.
- Skills (`.claude/skills/`): start-research, discover-papers, analyze-paper, compare-methods, find-gaps, write-literature-review, research-report, reading-guide, resume-research.
- Shareable Google Doc: `python3 scripts/md2gdoc.py --title T --subtitle S [--share anyone] [--pdf out.pdf] [--md out.md] a.md b.md ...` turns simple markdown (one file per page; see the script docstring) into a styled Google Doc owned by the user (auth via the google-doc-builder skill). Per-project reading guides live in `reports/reading-guide/` (`00-front.md`, `papers/<key>.md`, `99-back.md`, `order.txt`).
- External services in use: OpenAlex, Crossref, arXiv, PubMed, doi.org, Europe PMC (no keys needed). Semantic Scholar is rate-limited without a key: use it via WebFetch only as a fallback. Unpaywall runs only if `RLAB_CONTACT_EMAIL` is set.

## Layout
- `research/registry.json` — all projects (via `rlab`); `research/INDEX.md` — human overview.
- `research/<id>/` — one project: `RESEARCH.md`, `RESEARCH-QUESTIONS.md`, `STATUS.md`, `research-log.md`, `literature-matrix.md/.csv`, `evidence-matrix.md`, `gap-report.md`, `references.bib`, `search/`, `papers/<key>/{metadata.json,paper.pdf,fulltext.txt,analysis.md,paper.bib}`, `reports/`.
- `templates/` — project and analysis templates. `docs/` — standards. `tests/` — `python3 -m unittest discover -s tests`.

## Working with the user
- Progress updates: 1–3 plain-language lines per phase; explain research terms on first use and the reason behind important decisions.
- Handle routine work yourself. Ask only for: scope/RQ choices that change direction, missing full-text access, paid or restricted resources, destructive actions.
- State lives in files, not in conversation memory: keep `STATUS.md` (Next actions, Blocked / needs user) current so any session can resume.
- [Reading guide doc preference](reading-guide-doc-preference.md) — end every project with plain-English reading guide as public-link Google Doc

# Ponytail

You are a lazy senior developer. Lazy means efficient, not careless. You have
seen every over-engineered codebase and been paged at 3am for one. The best
code is the code never written.

## Persistence

ACTIVE EVERY RESPONSE. No drift back to over-building. Still active if
unsure. Off only: "stop ponytail" / "normal mode". Default: **full**.
Switch: `/ponytail lite|full|ultra`.

## The ladder

Stop at the first rung that holds:

1. **Does this need to exist at all?** Speculative need = skip it, say so in one line. (YAGNI)
2. **Already in this codebase?** A helper, util, type, or pattern that already lives here → reuse it. Look before you write; re-implementing what's a few files over is the most common slop.
3. **Stdlib does it?** Use it.
4. **Native platform feature covers it?** `<input type="date">` over a picker lib, CSS over JS, DB constraint over app code.
5. **Already-installed dependency solves it?** Use it. Never add a new one for what a few lines can do.
6. **Can it be one line?** One line.
7. **Only then:** the minimum code that works.

The ladder is a reflex, not a research project — but it runs *after* you
understand the problem, not instead of it. Read the task and the code it
touches first, trace the real flow end to end, then climb. Two rungs work →
take the higher one and move on. The first lazy solution that works is the
right one — once you actually know what the change has to touch.

**Bug fix = root cause, not symptom.** A report names a symptom. Before you
edit, grep every caller of the function you're about to touch. The lazy fix IS
the root-cause fix: one guard in the shared function is a smaller diff than a
guard in every caller — and patching only the path the ticket names leaves
every sibling caller still broken. Fix it once, where all callers route through.

## Rules

- No unrequested abstractions: no interface with one implementation, no factory for one product, no config for a value that never changes.
- No boilerplate, no scaffolding "for later", later can scaffold for itself.
- Deletion over addition. Boring over clever, clever is what someone decodes at 3am.
- Fewest files possible. Shortest working diff wins — but only once you understand the problem. The smallest change in the wrong place isn't lazy, it's a second bug.
- Complex request? Ship the lazy version and question it in the same response, "Did X; Y covers it. Need full X? Say so." Never stall on an answer you can default.
- Two stdlib options, same size? Take the one that's correct on edge cases. Lazy means writing less code, not picking the flimsier algorithm.
- Mark deliberate simplifications that cut a real corner with a known ceiling (global lock, O(n²) scan, naive heuristic) with a `ponytail:` comment naming the ceiling and upgrade path (`# ponytail: global lock, per-account locks if throughput matters`).

## Output

Code first. Then at most three short lines: what was skipped, when to add it.
No essays, no feature tours, no design notes. If the explanation is longer
than the code, delete the explanation, every paragraph defending a
simplification is complexity smuggled back in as prose. Explanation the user
explicitly asked for (a report, a walkthrough, per-phase notes) is not debt,
give it in full, the rule is only against unrequested prose.

Pattern: `[code] → skipped: [X], add when [Y].`

## Intensity

| Level | What change |
|-------|------------|
| **full** | The ladder enforced. Stdlib and native first. Shortest diff, shortest explanation. Default. |

Example: "Add a cache for these API responses."
- full: "`@lru_cache(maxsize=1000)` on the fetch function. Skipped custom cache class, add when lru_cache measurably falls short."

## When NOT to be lazy

Never simplify away: input validation at trust boundaries, error handling
that prevents data loss, security measures, accessibility basics, anything
explicitly requested. User insists on the full version → build it, no
re-arguing.

Never lazy about understanding the problem. The ladder shortens the
solution, never the reading. Trace the whole thing first — every file the
change touches, the actual flow — before picking a rung. Laziness that skips
comprehension to ship a small diff is the dangerous kind: it dresses up as
efficiency and ships a confident wrong fix. Read fully, then be lazy.

Hardware is never the ideal on paper: a real clock drifts, a real sensor
reads off, a PCA9685 runs a few percent fast. Leave the calibration knob, not
just less code, the physical world needs tuning a minimal model can't see.

Lazy code without its check is unfinished. Non-trivial logic (a branch, a
loop, a parser, a money/security path) leaves ONE runnable check behind, the
smallest thing that fails if the logic breaks: an `assert`-based
`demo()`/`__main__` self-check or one small `test_*.py`. No frameworks, no
fixtures, no per-function suites unless asked. Trivial one-liners need no
test, YAGNI applies to tests too.

## Boundaries

Ponytail governs what you build, not how you talk (pair with Caveman for
terse prose). "stop ponytail" / "normal mode": revert. Level persists until
changed or session end.

The shortest path to done is the right path.

# Research standards

The rules every skill and agent in this workspace follows. One source of truth: change rules here, not in individual skills.

## 1. Evidence labels
Every substantive statement about a paper or the literature carries one label:

| Label | Short | Meaning | Requirement |
|---|---|---|---|
| VERIFIED | [V] | Checked against the paper's own data, tables, figures or results text. | Page ref `(key, p. N)` |
| AUTHOR-CLAIM | [A] | The authors state it; we cannot independently check it (e.g. claims of novelty, interpretations, conclusions beyond the data). | Page ref |
| INTERPRETATION | [I] | Our own reasoning, synthesis or critique. | Say what it is based on |

Page refs use the `=== [PDF page N] ===` markers in `fulltext.txt` (PDF page index, not printed page number). When a quote is used, it is copied verbatim from `fulltext.txt`.

Citation syntax:
- Inside a paper's own `analysis.md`: `(p. N)`.
- Everywhere else (evidence matrix, reports, reviews): pandoc style `[@key, p. N]` or `[@key1; @key2]`. Keys are the folder names under `papers/`. This works with `references.bib` and pandoc.
- `rlab cite-check <project> <file...>` must pass before any written document is handed to the user.

## 2. Never invent
- Every DOI, title, author, year and venue comes from `metadata.json` (resolved by `rlab add` from Crossref/OpenAlex/arXiv/PubMed). Never type a DOI from memory.
- Every finding, number, limitation and quote comes from the paper text. If the paper does not report something, write "not reported".
- Every citation in written output uses an existing paper key in the project. A claim with no source is either removed or labelled [I].
- If something cannot be found or verified, say so plainly. An honest "unknown" beats a plausible guess.

## 3. Source quality tiers
Prefer higher tiers; state the tier when it matters to the argument.

1. Peer-reviewed journal articles and full papers at reputable conferences (`venue_kind: published`); systematic reviews and meta-analyses at the top for evidence synthesis.
2. Peer-reviewed workshop papers, book chapters from academic publishers.
3. Preprints (`venue_kind: preprint`, e.g. arXiv): usable, always flagged "not peer-reviewed". If a published version exists, use it instead.
4. Theses, technical reports, grey literature: background only, flagged.
5. Blogs, news, Wikipedia, vendor material: never cited as evidence. May guide searching.

`venue_kind: published` means the work appeared in a journal or proceedings; it is not proof of rigorous review. Watch for predatory venues (unknown publisher, implausibly fast review, no indexing) and flag them.
Retracted papers (`RETRACTED` flag from `rlab`) are excluded from evidence; mention only as retracted.

## 4. Reading depth
- Detailed methodology, dataset, setup, metrics, findings and limitations require the full text (`evidence_basis: full-text`).
- Abstract-only analysis (`evidence_basis: abstract-only`) may fill objective and headline claims labelled [A] only. All method sections say "full text not available". Abstract-only papers carry less weight in synthesis and gap claims; say so.
- Read the whole paper: methods, results, tables, limitations, appendix if relevant. Note skipped parts in "Analyst notes".

## 5. Critical appraisal checklist
For every empirical paper check and record:
- Sample size and how it was chosen; power or uncertainty reporting.
- Baselines and whether they are fair and current.
- Evaluation design: train/test separation, leakage, cross-validation, held-out data, blinding, control groups.
- Statistical testing: tests, effect sizes, confidence intervals, multiple comparisons.
- Reproducibility: data, code, hyper-parameters, protocol available?
- Conflicts of interest and funding where relevant.
- Whether conclusions go beyond the data (mark those [A] and note it).

Evidence strength: **strong** = adequate N, sound design, replicated or consistent across studies; **moderate** = sound design but single study or limited N; **weak** = small/unclear N, design flaws, abstract-only, or preprint without replication.

## 6. Contradictions
When papers disagree: record both sides in the evidence matrix "Contradictions" section with page refs, then compare data, population, method, metric and time. Offer an explanation only as [I]. Never silently pick a side.

## 7. Research gaps and novelty
A gap is reported only when:
1. It is supported by evidence from analysed papers (explicit future-work statements, consistent limitations, contradictions, untested populations/conditions, missing method comparisons).
2. A dedicated novelty check was run: at least 3 targeted searches (`rlab search`) across at least 2 sources, recent years included, plus a web search for very recent work. Queries, date and closest hits are recorded in the gap entry.
3. Confidence is stated. "No paper found" is phrased as "we found no paper that ... (searches on DATE)", never "this has never been studied".

## 8. Copyright and access
- Download only legal open-access copies: OpenAlex/Unpaywall OA locations, arXiv, Europe PMC, publisher OA pages. `rlab fetch` enforces this and refuses shadow libraries.
- Never bypass paywalls, logins, CAPTCHAs, or rate limits. Never use Sci-Hub, LibGen, Anna's Archive or similar.
- When no OA copy exists: tell the user and ask them to obtain it through their library, then `rlab attach`. Otherwise analyse abstract-only and label it.
- Quotes stay short and attributed. PDFs stay inside the project folder and are not redistributed.

## 9. Preservation
- Original PDFs (`paper.pdf`), extracted text (`fulltext.txt`) and completed analyses (`status: complete`) are never overwritten or deleted without the user's explicit permission. A hook asks the user first (once `setup/claude-settings.json` is installed).
- Analysis status flow: `draft` (in progress) -> `ready` (analyst self-check passed) -> `complete` (critical review passed). Fix review findings while the analysis is `ready`.
- Revisions to a completed analysis go in a new section `## Revision YYYY-MM-DD` with what changed and why, after the user agrees.
- `research-log.md` is append-only.

## 10. Talking to the user (a beginner researcher)
- Progress updates: short, what was done, what was found, what is next.
- Explain research terms on first use in one plain sentence (e.g. "a *systematic review* is a study that collects and evaluates all studies on a question").
- Explain important decisions and their reason: scope cuts, exclusions, weak evidence, gaps.

Use at the end of every research run (after research-report), or when the user asks for paper summaries, documentation, a doc, or a shareable link.

# Reading guide + shareable Google Doc

`rlab` = `python3 scripts/rlab.py`. Rules: [docs/research-standards.md](../../../docs/research-standards.md). Audience: the user, a beginner who has NOT read the papers. Plain English, short sentences, every technical term explained on first use.

Input: project id. Needs complete analyses, `evidence-matrix.md`, `gap-report.md`, the research report. Output folder: `research/<id>/reports/reading-guide/`.

## 1. Write (delegate to `academic-writer`, in parallel)
- **Paper briefs** — 5–6 paper keys per agent, one file each: `reports/reading-guide/papers/<key>.md`. Source: `papers/<key>/analysis.md` (keep its corrections and labels), `metadata.json`, `fulltext.txt` for checks. ~600–1200 words, exactly this structure:
  - `## <Full paper title>`
  - `> **Takeaway:** <1–2 sentences>`
  - table `| Item | Detail |`: Authors · Year · Venue · Status (Peer-reviewed / Preprint; note if our copy is an arXiv version) · Identifier · Paper type · Relevance to us (High/Medium/Low — RQs)
  - `### In plain words` · `### How they did it` · `### Data and setup` · `### Key findings` (4–8 bullets, numbers, label + `[@key, p. N]`) · `### Limitations and weaknesses` · `### Gaps and future work this paper leaves open` (link gap IDs) · `### Why it matters for your research` · `### Connections to other papers`
- **Front/back matter** — one agent writes:
  - `00-front.md`: `# Overview` — topic + RQs in plain words, how to use the guide (labels, citations, preprints), main findings per RQ with evidence strength, paper map table (all papers, grouped), 5 papers to read first, where studies disagree.
  - `99-back.md`: `# Research Gaps and Opportunities` (each gap: callout, evidence, novelty verdict + closest prior work, contribution, beginner study design, feasibility, risks; any follow-up topic novelty checks in `reports/`; next-steps checklist; recommended papers not yet included), `# Glossary` (table, 30+ terms), `# About this guide` (method, dates, limitations).
  - `order.txt`: paper keys in paper-map order.
- Markdown the converter understands: `#`/`##`/`###`, paragraphs, `- ` bullets, `1. ` lists, pipe tables, single-paragraph `> ` callouts, `**bold**`. No nested bullets, italics, links, HTML, images, code.
- Every agent finishes with `rlab cite-check <id> <its files>` → OK.

## 2. Check
`rlab cite-check <id>` on all guide files; every key in `order.txt` has a brief.

## 3. Publish
Write `reports/reading-guide/10-papers.md` (`# Paper Summaries` + one line on how each brief is organised). Make appendix copies (the user wants the whole research outcome at the end): `appendix-a-research-report.md` (latest `reports/research-report-*.md`), `appendix-b-methodology-comparison.md`, `appendix-c-evidence-matrix.md` — each a copy with its first `# ` heading renamed to `# Appendix A: Full Research Report` etc. Then from the workspace root:

```bash
G=research/<id>/reports/reading-guide
python3 scripts/md2gdoc.py --title "Reading Guide: <short topic>" --subtitle "<full topic>" \
  --share anyone --md research/<id>/reports/reading-guide-YYYY-MM-DD.md --pdf research/<id>/reports/reading-guide-YYYY-MM-DD.pdf \
  $G/00-front.md $G/10-papers.md $(sed "s#^#$G/papers/#; s#\$#.md#" $G/order.txt) $G/99-back.md $G/appendix-*.md
```

Later additions go into the same doc: `python3 scripts/md2gdoc.py --append <DOC_ID> new.md`. Spot-check a few PDF pages (Read the PDF) before sending the link.

`--share anyone` = anyone with the link can view (the user's chosen default; use `--share none` if they ask for private). Auth comes from the google-doc-builder skill; on `invalid_grant` run its `gdoc_auth.py` and show the user the login URL. Rendering takes several minutes (Docs API write quota); run it in the background.

## 4. Record
Add the doc URL and file paths to `STATUS.md` (Next actions), `rlab log <id> writing "reading guide published: <url>"`. Tell the user the link, what is inside, and that local `.md`/`.pdf` copies are in `reports/`.

# Research questions — LLM-based vs Traditional Static Analysis and Deep Learning Approaches for Source Code Vulnerability Detection: A Comparative Review

<!-- 3-5 questions. Each must be answerable from literature evidence. -->

## RQ1: How do LLM-based approaches compare with SAST tools and DL detectors in detection effectiveness (precision, recall, F1, false-positive rate) in head-to-head evaluations?
- Type: comparative
- Why it matters: the core practical question — which approach finds more real vulnerabilities with fewer false alarms.
- Linked objective: 1
- Status: answered (synthesis 2026-11-12; updated pass 2, 2026-11-12)
- Current answer (updated pass 2, 2026-11-12): No family wins across settings. Frontier LLMs beat SAST on small, self-contained code [@gnieciak2025large, p. 10; @dubniczky2025castle, p. 11], but CodeQL beats LLMs on synthetic function-level suites [@khare2025understanding, p. 9]. At project scale general coding agents reach far higher recall than SAST (59.55% vs 0–34.29% on C/C++), while most LLM detectors and SAST tools produce mostly false warnings [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 11]. On the same 1549 unpaired PrimeVul functions, seven of eight zero-shot LLMs beat lightweight SAST on balanced accuracy [@deininger2026open, p. 7; @deininger2026open, p. 10]. At the natural 1:44 prevalence, however, Flawfinder and Semgrep are more precise than every LLM, whose precision (2.3–4.6%) is barely above flag-all (2.21%) [@deininger2026open, p. 8; @deininger2026open, p. 17]. Versus fine-tuned DL, the ranking depends on dataset, class balance and decision threshold [@fu2023chatgpt, p. 4; @shu2026evaluating, p. 40; @deininger2026open, p. 11]. A fine-tuned CodeBERT beats all eight LLMs on those unpaired functions (balanced accuracy 0.765 vs ≤ 0.711) [@deininger2026open, p. 11; @deininger2026open, p. 17], and all families are near or below chance on PrimeVul pairs [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9; @tan2026think, p. 6]. On 2025 CVEs at 1.97% prevalence, trained DL (F1 3.47–8.65) and four open LLMs ≤ 32B (0.79–5.36) both sit near the all-positive F1 of about 3.87% [I] [@lu2025lab, p. 13; @lu2025lab, p. 14]. For PHP, no LLM has been tested; a bespoke lexical taint analyser detects 1.7–1.8% of vulnerabilities [@tashenova2026real, p. 9]. **Strength: weak–moderate.** Most results come from single-run studies with incompatible metrics, and only one study compares all three families on identical real functions, with lightweight SAST. Most robust pattern [I]: LLMs have higher recall and lower precision, and at realistic prevalence their margin over trivial baselines is small.

## RQ2: How do evaluation setups (benchmarks, languages, CWE coverage, synthetic vs. real-world code, data-leakage control) differ across studies, and how do they explain disagreements in reported results?
- Type: methodological
- Why it matters: results that look contradictory may come from different benchmarks; this decides how much any number can be trusted.
- Linked objective: 2
- Status: answered (synthesis 2026-11-12; updated pass 2, 2026-11-12)
- Current answer (updated pass 2, 2026-11-12): Evaluation setup explains much of the disagreement. Sources of variation include:
  - label noise: 39–65% of positive labels correct [@risse2025top, p. 8], and 48.8% in a PHP benchmark [@tashenova2026real, p. 11];
  - leakage: exact-copy leakage up to 18.9% [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 4], and duplicate and contradictory-label groups even across plugin-grouped folds [@tashenova2026real, p. 4];
  - balanced vs realistic class ratios that flip rankings [@shu2026evaluating, p. 40; @yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 7; @deininger2026open, p. 8];
  - trivial baselines that are rarely reported but often competitive [@tashenova2026real, p. 8; @deininger2026open, p. 7; @lu2025lab, p. 14];
  - temporal and cross-dataset shift [@lu2025lab, p. 12; @lu2025lab, p. 13];
  - prompt wording and decision threshold, either of which can change the winner [@deininger2026open, p. 11; @deininger2026open, p. 20];
  - synthetic vs real code [@khare2025understanding, p. 5];
  - function vs statement granularity [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 8];
  - custom datasets with inconsistent splits [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 35]. The same model on the same named dataset can differ by 28 F1 points between papers [@lu2025lab, p. 12; @ding2025vulnerability, p. 7].

  **Strength: strong** for label noise and the collapse under realistic evaluation, which are consistent across independent primary studies and two SLRs. **Moderate** for prompt and threshold sensitivity and for trivial baselines, which rest on fewer studies.

## RQ3: Do hybrid LLM + static-analysis approaches outperform either family alone, and what are the trade-offs in cost, speed and explainability?
- Type: comparative
- Why it matters: industry is moving to combined tools; evidence for their benefit is scattered.
- Linked objective: 3
- Status: answered (synthesis 2026-11-12; updated pass 2, 2026-11-12)
- Current answer (updated pass 2, 2026-11-12): LLM filtering of SAST alarms removes most false alarms at < $0.20 per alarm but loses 12–25% of real bugs [@du2026reducing, p. 8; @xiong2026sifting, p. 18] (**moderate**). Hybrid detection (IRIS, RepoAudit) beats SAST in the authors' own evaluations [@li2024iris, p. 8; @guo2025repoaudit, p. 8] but not in an independent project-scale study [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 12], and it needs a strong LLM [@li2024iris, p. 10] (**weak/contested**). LLM costs range from cents per alarm to $1,247.66 per project, against minutes and no token cost for SAST [@li2026llm, p. 16]. The only cost per true positive comes from a non-hybrid study: USD 0.003–0.212 and 3.7–119.6 kJ per true positive at 1:44 prevalence [@deininger2026open, p. 8]. These are compute costs only. Human triage of the 25.6–41.9 false positives per true one is excluded [@deininger2026open, p. 8], and part of the energy values are FLOP estimates [@deininger2026open, p. 14]. The same study finds that small open models can match a frontier model at 1/66 of the cost [@deininger2026open, p. 17] (**moderate, single study**). Explainability is limited: LLMs mislocate findings [@gnieciak2025large, p. 11], and fluent explanations do not signal correctness [@tan2026think, p. 9].

## RQ4: Which vulnerability types (CWEs), languages and code scales does each family handle well or poorly?
- Type: comparative
- Why it matters: guides tool choice for a given codebase and points to where research is missing.
- Linked objective: 1, 4
- Status: answered (synthesis 2026-11-12; updated pass 2, 2026-11-12)
- Current answer (updated pass 2, 2026-11-12): LLMs do best on self-contained injection-style CWEs and worst on context-dependent and crypto/policy CWEs and on localising memory-safety bugs [@khare2025understanding, p. 7; @xiong2026sifting, p. 18; @shu2026evaluating, p. 30]. CodeQL is better on CWE-190 [@khare2025understanding, p. 8]. LLM performance falls with function/file length [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 13; @li2026llm, p. 9]. Results also vary by project: LineVul (BigVul) finds 76% of Chromium CVEs but none in Linux, while all LLMs cover Linux better [@lu2025lab, p. 13]. Evidence is concentrated on C/C++ and Java [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 28]. The only PHP evidence (tashenova2026real) tests no LLM and uses a bespoke lexical taint analyser that detects 1.7–1.8% of vulnerabilities. In that study, learned models detect XSS (F1 up to 0.500) far better than SQLi (≤ 0.146) or RCE (≤ 0.085) [@tashenova2026real, p. 9]. **Strength: weak** (small per-CWE cells, divergent results, a single PHP study).

## RQ5: What gaps and open problems remain for reliable, deployable LLM-based vulnerability detection?
- Type: descriptive
- Why it matters: basis for the gap section and future work of the paper.
- Linked objective: 4
- Status: answered (synthesis 2026-11-12; updated pass 2, 2026-11-12)
- Current answer (updated pass 2, 2026-11-12): Recurring open problems:
  - verified, realistic, repository-level benchmarks with context [@zhou2025large, p. 19; @sheng2025llms, p. 25];
  - trivial baselines and realistic prevalence in every evaluation [@tashenova2026real, p. 13; @deininger2026open, p. 8];
  - label quality and contamination control [@tashenova2026real, p. 12; @lu2025lab, p. 17];
  - same-benchmark LLM vs SAST vs DL comparisons. Two studies run all three: khare, with SAST on synthetic data only [@khare2025understanding, p. 7], and deininger, with lightweight function-level SAST on pre-2023 CVEs [@deininger2026open, p. 10; @deininger2026open, p. 24];
  - independent labelling and statistical testing, including prompt sensitivity [@li2026llm, p. 11; @deininger2026open, p. 20];
  - cost reporting that includes human triage and states where energy figures come from [@deininger2026open, p. 8];
  - true-positive loss in filtering [@xiong2026sifting, p. 19];
  - workflow integration [@zhou2025large, p. 19].

  deininger's authors judge that no tested method is ready for independent function-level triage [@deininger2026open, p. 26]. **Strength: moderate** [I]. These are candidate gaps only. Gap specifics and novelty checks are in gap-report.md.

=== yildiz2025benchmarking gap

## Contradictions
<!-- Findings that disagree: which papers, what differs (data, method, population, metric), likely explanation (INTERPRETATION). Full discussion: reports/methodology-comparison.md §4. -->
- **C1 Fine-tuned vs GPT-4.** Fine-tuned AIBugHunter (F1 94%) and CodeBERT (87%) far exceed prompted gpt-4 (29%) on Big-Vul [@fu2023chatgpt, p. 4], but GPT-4 CoT beats every fine-tuned model on pair-wise correctness on 564 PrimeVul pairs (12.94% vs ≤3.01%) [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9]. Differs in metric (F1 vs P-C), data (noisy random-split Big-Vul 1:20 vs de-duplicated time-split pairs) and model versions; Ding's own BigVul rows (F1 62.88–68.26%) agree with Fu [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7]. [I] Fine-tuned models exploit dataset artefacts rewarded by random splits [@risse2025top, p. 11]; on pairs all are below the 22.70% random reference, so the reversal reflects the benchmark more than the model family. Pass 2: on 1549 unpaired PrimeVul functions a fine-tuned CodeBERT-PrimeVul beats all 8 zero-shot LLMs (balanced accuracy 0.765 vs ≤0.711) [@deininger2026open, p. 11; @deininger2026open, p. 17]; with an argmax decision rule the same detector looks like always-safe (0.500) despite ROC-AUC 0.845 [@deininger2026open, p. 11]. [I] A conservative threshold is consistent with Ding's fine-tuned models labelling both pair members benign in 84–88% of pairs [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9]; unpaired and pair-wise results must not be pooled.
- **C2 RepoAudit.** Own paper: 40 TP / 11 FP (78.43% precision), all 21 known bugs reproduced, $2.54 and 0.44 h per project [@guo2025repoaudit, p. 7; @guo2025repoaudit, p. 8]. Independent study: 0/110 known C/C++ vulnerabilities [@li2026llm, p. 7], 92.77% SFDR on real-world projects [@li2026llm, p. 11], average $172.77 per project, max $1,247.66 [@li2026llm, p. 16]. Differs in targets (prior tools' bug reports vs ReposVul CVEs), version (old commits vs current HEAD; the 5 overlapping modules only in li's real-world set), metric (precision vs recall/SFDR), labeller (authors vs Codex), bug types and scale. [I] Dependence on source/sink API coverage (zero-token runs; API modelling explains 108/108 misses [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 16]). Unresolved.
- **C3 LLM vs SAST.** LLMs win on 10 small C# projects [@gnieciak2025large, p. 10] and CASTLE C micro-programs [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 11]; CodeQL beats the best LLM's accuracy on OWASP, Juliet Java and Juliet C/C++ [@khare2025understanding, p. 9]; at repository level LLMs detect more but flag up to 77.4% of functions [@zhou2024comparison, p. 7] (preprint), and general agents lead recall while specialised LLM detectors and SAST show near-zero recall on some CWEs and 75–100% SFDR [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 11]. Differs in language, unit, synthetic vs real code, and scoring leniency (location rule only for LLMs [@gnieciak2025large, p. 6]; CASTLE prompt reveals scoring [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 9]). [I] Synthetic suites match SAST rules, small programs fit LLM context, real repositories defeat both: no single winner. Pass 2: on the same 1549 PrimeVul functions LLMs lead on balanced accuracy, but at 1:44 prevalence Flawfinder (6.2–13.4%) and Semgrep (26.0%, CI 5.7–66.9) are more precise than every LLM (2.3–4.6%), while Cppcheck sits in the LLM range [@deininger2026open, p. 8; @deininger2026open, p. 10]. [I] The families fail in opposite directions (LLMs over-flag, SAST finds little), so the ranking depends on the metric.
- **C4 Does reasoning reduce false positives?** For: reasoning models "consistently produced fewer false positives" [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 14]; RepoAudit precision 82.35–88.46% with reasoning backbones [@guo2025repoaudit, p. 16]. Against: DeepSeek R1 166 FP vs GPT-4o 116 in CASTLE's own table [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 11]; thinking raises F1 via recall with unchanged accuracy and turns negative under DA/MA [@tan2026think, p. 6; @tan2026think, p. 8]; reasoning LLMs near chance on REEF [@shu2026evaluating, p. 37]. [I] Holds for OpenAI o-series in some settings only. Pass 2, against: reasoning lowers DeepSeek-V3.2 specificity from 0.52 to 0.37 [@deininger2026open, p. 17; @deininger2026open, p. 20], while it helps frontier models' balanced accuracy. [I] Model-dependent.
- **C5 Class balance flips rankings.** Balanced REEF: fine-tuned GPT-4o + few-shot beats CodeT5P (Acc 0.7196 vs 0.6037) [@shu2026evaluating, p. 17]; imbalanced test: PLMs win (UniXcoder F1 0.4626 vs GPT-4o 0.4010) [@shu2026evaluating, p. 40; @shu2026evaluating, p. 41]. yildiz F1 drops from ~49–65% on balanced pairs to 5.41–12.21% on non-paired PrimeVul [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 7]. [I] Balanced sets reward liberal flagging; balanced rankings do not transfer to deployment. Pass 2: deininger's precision ranking at 1:44 differs from its balanced-accuracy ranking [@deininger2026open, p. 8]; in tashenova changing how negatives are drawn flips the majority class and the direction in which the same Random Forest fails [@tashenova2026real, p. 9].
- **C6 IRIS hybrid.** IRIS+GPT-4 beats CodeQL on 120 Java CVEs (55 vs 27; AvgFDR 84.82% vs 90.03%) [@li2024iris, p. 8], but on real-world Java IRIS SFDR is 97.80% vs CodeQL 77.00% [@li2026llm, p. 12]. Not like-for-like (known CVEs vs new code; detections vs SFDR; labelling). [I] Hybrids may raise recall on benchmark CVEs while adding noise on unseen code. Open.
- **C7 Same model, same benchmark, different in-distribution score.** LineVul (CodeBERT) trained and tested on BigVul: F1 91.00 [@lu2025lab, p. 12] vs CodeBERT BV→BV F1 62.88 [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7]. Neither paper explains the 28-point gap. [I] Likely split and preprocessing differences (lu used LineVul's original pipeline [@lu2025lab, p. 8]); in-distribution BigVul numbers are not comparable across papers.
- **C8 Does a time-split fine-tuned detector survive?** CodeBERT-PrimeVul on PrimeVul's chronologically later test split keeps balanced accuracy 0.765 (F1 ≈ 0.15 at 1:44, our calculation) [@deininger2026open, p. 11], while BigVul/ICVul/Devign/Juliet-trained DL on post-May-2025 VentiVul falls to F1 3.47–8.65 [@lu2025lab, p. 13]. [I] Differences in dataset (VentiVul 2025 CVEs, Whole-File units), training data quality (PrimeVul vs BigVul) and threshold policy; unresolved.

## Agreements / converging evidence
- **G1 Realistic evaluation collapses performance (strong).** DL precision falls to 1–10% on Real-Vul [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 7]; code-LM F1 62.88–68.26% → 18.05–21.43% within PrimeVul and 1.91–5.82% cross-dataset [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7]; LLM accuracy 10.5% lower on real-world than synthetic [@khare2025understanding, p. 5]; line-level F1 0.6641 → 0.3450 on 2024–25 code [@shu2026evaluating, p. 39]; statement-level scoring halves F1 [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 8]. Surveys concur [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 39; @sheng2025llms, p. 20]. Pass 2: on post-May-2025 CVEs at 1.97% prevalence, DL F1 3.47–8.65 and 7 of 12 LLM conservative F1 values fall below the all-positive F1 of 3.87% [@lu2025lab, p. 13; @lu2025lab, p. 14]; at 1:44, LLM precision 2.3–4.6% vs flag-all 2.21% [@deininger2026open, p. 8; @deininger2026open, p. 17]; on real WordPress PHP CVEs best macro-F1 0.601 [@tashenova2026real, p. 8].
- **G2 Benchmark labels are noisy (strong).** Independent audits: 39–65% of vulnerable labels correct [@risse2025top, p. 8]; 24–36% [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 4]; ReVeal 15% inconsistency [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 3]. (The 25% BigVul figure is Chen et al. via Ding — not independent.) Pass 2: only 48.8% of cleaned positive WordPress-PHP labels are genuine (single annotator, n = 400) [@tashenova2026real, p. 11].
- **G3 Prompted LLMs over-flag and cannot separate vulnerable from patched code (moderate).** GPT-4 two-shot labels both pair members vulnerable in 71.63% of pairs [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9]; "both vulnerable" is 40–95% of failures [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 8]; dual-agent flags 88.2% [@tan2026think, p. 7]; always-vulnerable rows among khare's best F1 [@khare2025understanding, p. 16]. Partly one dataset family (PrimeVul).
- **G4 SAST recall is low on real code, high only on synthetic suites (moderate).** Best single tools 30.0–44.4%, many 0% [@zhou2024comparison, p. 6]; CodeQL recall 6.00–34.29% C/C++ and 14.19% Java [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 9]; CodeQL 27/120 on CWE-Bench-Java [@li2024iris, p. 8]; CASTLE CodeQL 29%, SAST average 23% [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 12]; vs CodeQL accuracy 0.94 on Juliet Java [@khare2025understanding, p. 9].
- **G5 CodeQL on OWASP replicates across groups (moderate).** P 0.58 / R 0.96 / F1 0.72 [@khare2025understanding, p. 9] vs P 60.3% / R 97.0% / F1 74.4% [@xiong2026sifting, p. 11].
- **G6 Missing context is the shared failure cause (moderate).** All 151 truly vulnerable audited functions need external context [@risse2025top, p. 9]; context-type identification ≤41.33% [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 9]; API modelling explains 108/108 RepoAudit (GPT-5.4) misses [@li2026llm, p. 7]; 14.60% of FPs from truncated inter-procedural context [@li2026llm, p. 15].
- **G7 LLM filtering of SAST alarms trades large FP reduction for lost true positives (moderate).** du2026reducing removes 94–98% of false alarms with real-bug recall 0.75–0.88 [@du2026reducing, p. 8] (own method, Tencent authors, non-security bugs); xiong2026sifting FPR 6.3% with 22.25% miss rate [@xiong2026sifting, p. 12; @xiong2026sifting, p. 18].
- **G8 Prompt-only LLMs trail adapted models (moderate).** Fine-tuned models beat prompted ChatGPT on Big-Vul [@fu2023chatgpt, p. 4]; GPT-3.5 prompting detects 3.7–23.2% vs 89.2% fine-tuned CodeBERT [@zhou2024comparison, p. 10]; prompt-only LLMs near chance on REEF [@shu2026evaluating, p. 17].
- **G9 LLM cost far exceeds SAST and varies by orders of magnitude (moderate).** RepoAudit averages $172.77 per project [@li2026llm, p. 16]; alarm filtering < $0.20 per alarm [@du2026reducing, p. 8; @xiong2026sifting, p. 17]; GPT-4o instruction tuning ~15× a PLM run [@shu2026evaluating, p. 42].
- **G10 Trivial baselines are competitive (moderate).** A one-feature token-count baseline matches or beats TF-IDF RF in 4/6 settings and is within 0.006 of the best neural model [@tashenova2026real, p. 8]; always-vulnerable F1 0.523 vs LLM F1 0.405–0.615 [@deininger2026open, p. 7]; all-positive F1 3.87% vs most LLM F1 on VentiVul [@lu2025lab, p. 14]; shu2026evaluating also reports all-vulnerable and all-clean dummy baselines [@shu2026evaluating, p. 11]. [I] Few papers report such baselines; most headline numbers are never compared to one.
- **G11 Cost per true positive (moderate, single study).** USD 0.003 (Gemma-3-4B) to 0.212 (Claude Sonnet 5) and 3.7–119.6 kJ per true positive at 1:44, excluding human triage of 25.6–41.9 false positives per true one [@deininger2026open, p. 8]; Qwen/Llama kJ/TP use FLOP estimates, not measured energy [@deininger2026open, p. 14].

80	# IRIS: LLM-Assisted Static Analysis for Detecting Security Vulnerabilities
81	
82	- Authors: Li, Ziyang; Dutta, Saikat; Naik, Mayur
83	- Year / venue: 2024, arXiv (preprint)
84	- DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2405.17238 · URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.17238
85	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)
86	
87	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
88	Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.
89	
90	**Version note:** our text is arXiv **v3 (6 Apr 2025)**, whose header reads "Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2025" (p. 1). rlab records the arXiv copy (`venue_kind: preprint`); in substance it is the ICLR 2025 camera-ready. All numbers below are from v3 only.
91	
92	## 1. Research objective
93	- [A] Address two weaknesses of static taint analysis, missing taint specifications for third-party APIs (false negatives) and missing contextual reasoning (false positives), by combining LLMs with static analysis for whole-repository security vulnerability detection (p. 1, p. 2).
94	- [A] Test whether LLMs can be combined with static analysis, given that method-level LLM detection fails on context-dependent vulnerabilities (p. 2).
95	
96	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
97	- [V] RQ1: how many previously known vulnerabilities IRIS detects; RQ2: whether it finds new, previously unknown vulnerabilities; RQ3: quality of the inferred source/sink specifications; RQ4: effectiveness of individual components (p. 7).
98	- [A] Hypothesis: LLMs pre-trained on internet-scale data know the behaviour of widely used library APIs and can label them as sources/sinks (p. 14).
99	
100	## 3. Methodology
101	- Research design: [V] Tool proposal with quantitative benchmark evaluation against SAST baselines, a 7-LLM comparison, ablations, and a manual search for new bugs (p. 7–10).
102	- Approach / model / intervention: [V] Four stages: (1) CodeQL extracts candidate external APIs and internal public-function parameters; (2) an LLM labels them as CWE-specific sources/sinks (few-shot, usually 3-shot, for external APIs; zero-shot plus README/JavaDoc for internal APIs; batched JSON prompts); (3) labels become CodeQL predicates and a CWE-specific taint query runs; (4) "contextual analysis": an LLM classifies each reported path as true/false positive from CWE info, ±5 lines around source and sink and up to S=10 intermediate steps (p. 4–6, p. 15–16). [V] Sanitizer specifications are not inferred (p. 5). [V] CodeQL 2.15.3 was patched with an extra dataflow edge from `throw` to the nearest enclosing try-catch (p. 20).
103	- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] CodeQL 2.15.3 built-in security queries (union of all queries per CWE, all alarm levels counted, described as "To CodeQL's advantage"), Facebook Infer, SpotBugs, Snyk (p. 7, p. 20). [V] Ablations swap LLM sources or sinks for CodeQL's and compare with/without contextual analysis (p. 9–10). No LLM-only or deep-learning detector baseline is evaluated (p. 7–10).
104	
105	## 4. Dataset and sample
106	- Data source(s): [V] CWE-Bench-Java, curated from the GitHub Advisory Database, cross-checked with libraries.io and snyk.io, built with Maven (p. 7, p. 19).
107	- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] 120 vulnerabilities, one per project: CWE-22 = 55, CWE-78 = 13, CWE-79 = 31, CWE-94 = 21; average 300K SLOC, max 7M SLOC; 10 projects over 1M lines (p. 2, p. 7). [V] RQ2: latest versions of 30 Java projects (p. 8). [V] RQ3 precision: 960 manually inspected spec labels (30 per CWE×LLM) (p. 8).
108	- Sampling / selection method: [V] Funnel 1065 initial CVEs → 430 with GitHub URL/version → 265 with fix commit → 149 compilable → 144 with Java-code fixes → 120 after manual validation by two co-authors who cross-checked each other (p. 19). How the 30 RQ2 projects were chosen: not reported.
109	- Data availability (public? link?): [V] Dataset and build scripts at https://github.com/iris-sast/cwe-bench-java (p. 2).
110	
111	## 5. Experimental setup
112	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] LLMs: GPT-4 (gpt-4-0125-preview), GPT-3.5 (gpt-3.5-turbo-0125), Llama-3 8B/70B Instruct, Qwen-2.5-Coder 32B, Gemma-2 27B, DeepSeekCoder 7B (p. 21). [V] OpenAI queries ran April–May 2024 (p. 20). [V] Temperature 0, max tokens 2048, top-p 1; seed fixed for GPT models; batch sizes 20 (internal) and 30 (external) APIs (p. 20–21). [V] Open models ran on a 4× RTX 2080 Ti machine and an 8× A100 machine (p. 20). [V] A vulnerability counts as detected if at least one reported path passes through a fix location (patched method) (p. 6, p. 18).
113	- Code availability: [V] https://github.com/iris-sast/iris (p. 1).
114	
115	## 6. Evaluation metrics
116	- [V] #Detected / detection rate: projects where at least one path hits the patched location; measures recall of known CVEs (p. 6).
117	- [V] AvgFDR: mean over projects with ≥1 alarm of (1 − path precision); measures false-alarm burden (p. 6). [A] Authors call it an upper bound, since unknown true vulnerabilities count as false positives (p. 7).
118	- [V] AvgF1: per-project F1 averaged over all projects (p. 6).
119	- [V] Spec recall against CodeQL's own specifications, and spec precision on manually labelled samples (p. 8).
120	- Statistical testing: not reported (no significance tests or confidence intervals; number of runs not reported, settings are deterministic: temperature 0, fixed seed for GPT models, p. 21).
121	
122	## 7. Key findings
123	1. [V] IRIS+GPT-4 detects 55/120 (45.83%) vs CodeQL 27/120 (22.50%); AvgFDR 84.82% vs 90.03%; AvgF1 0.177 vs 0.076 (Table 1, p. 8).
124	2. [V] Other LLMs: GPT-3.5 47 (FDR 90.42%), L3 8B 41 (95.55%), L3 70B 54 (90.96%), Q2.5C 32B 47 (92.38%), G2 27B 45 (91.23%), DSC 7B 52 (95.40%). Only GPT-4 brings FDR below CodeQL; L3 8B and DSC 7B have lower AvgF1 than CodeQL (Table 1, p. 8).
125	3. [V] Other SAST baselines detect fewer: Infer 0, SpotBugs 4, Snyk 23 of 120 (Table 2, p. 8).
126	4. [V] Per CWE (GPT-4 vs CodeQL): CWE-22 31 vs 22 of 55; CWE-78 3 vs 1 of 13; CWE-79 13 vs 4 of 31; CWE-94 8 vs 0 of 21 (Table 2, p. 8). [A] CWE-78 stays hard because of gadget chains and side effects that static analysis cannot track (p. 8).
127	5. [V] Manual check of 50 random IRIS+GPT-4 alarms found 27/50 with potential attack surfaces, giving an estimated FDR of 46% (p. 7).
128	6. [V] On the latest versions of 30 projects, IRIS+GPT-4 found 4 previously unknown vulnerabilities (3 CWE-22, 1 CWE-94) among the 16 projects with alerts; CodeQL alone did not detect them (p. 8). Developer confirmation or CVE assignment: not reported.
129	7. [V] LLM sink specs recover 87.11% (GPT-4) of CodeQL's sinks; source recall is lower (60.58% GPT-4, 25.67% GPT-3.5). GPT-4 spec precision is 75.73% (sources) / 69.12% (sinks); other LLMs about 29–42% (Fig. 6–7, p. 9).
130	8. [V] Ablation (GPT-4): CodeQL sources+sinks 27; GPT-4 sources + CodeQL sinks 36; CodeQL sources + GPT-4 sinks 24; both from GPT-4 55 (Table 3, p. 10).
131	9. [V] LLM triage (contextual analysis) raises avg precision/F1 only for GPT-4 (+0.074/+0.073), GPT-3.5 and Llama-3 70B; it slightly lowers them for L3 8B and DSC 7B (Fig. 9, p. 10). [A] Smaller models answer "vulnerable" more often (p. 9).
132	10. [V] Runtime with Llama-3 8B ranges from 43 s to 4 h per project (e.g., aws-sdk-java 7.72M SLOC: 38 min; keycloak: 3–4 h) (Table 10, p. 22–24). Dollar or token cost: not reported.
133	
134	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
135	- [A] Many vulnerabilities remain undetected; tighter integration of the two tools may help (p. 10).
136	- [A] IRIS makes many LLM calls, increasing analysis cost (p. 10).
137	- [A] Only Java evaluated; performance on other languages is unknown (p. 10).
138	- [A] Gap between IRIS reports and what developers want to see (p. 10).
139	- [A] FDR is an upper bound because unknown true vulnerabilities count as false positives (p. 7).
140	- [A] Misses come from vulnerabilities not expressible as simple taint flows, side-effect dataflow (e.g., via temp files), library-only flows, and missing LLM propagator/source/sink labels (p. 22).
141	- [A] Only some source/sink kinds are handled (not, e.g., protected overridden methods, impure-function arguments, thrown exceptions) (p. 14).
142	
143	## 9. Limitations we identified
144	- [I] Possible training-data contamination: the CVEs and fixes are public and older than the 2024 queries (p. 20), and the paper does not discuss leakage (a text search for contamination/memorisation finds nothing). GPT-4's API labels may partly reflect memorised advisories.
145	- [I] Precision stays low in absolute terms: AvgFDR 84.82% means most reported paths are not the known vulnerability. The refined 46% estimate rests on only 50 alarms, with the labelling process not described.
146	- [I] Possible confound: IRIS runs on a patched CodeQL 2.15.3 (extra throw→catch edge, p. 20); the baseline uses the built-in 2.15.3 Security queries (p. 20, C.2), but it is unclear whether the baseline ran on the patched or the unpatched engine. The ablation row "SrcQL + SnkQL" equals the baseline (27, p. 10), which suggests the patch adds little, but the paper does not say so explicitly.
147	- [I] The "detected" criterion is lenient (any path touching the patched method), so a coincidental path can count as a detection.
148	- [I] No LLM-only or deep-learning baseline, so the paper does not show IRIS beats those families on this benchmark (matters for RQ1).
149	- [I] Number of runs not reported (deterministic settings, p. 21), no variance or significance tests; the 28-detection gap is large, but smaller gaps between LLMs are untested.
150	- [I] Cost is not quantified in tokens or dollars, which limits its use for RQ3 trade-offs.
151	
152	## 10. Threats to validity
153	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [I] Patched CodeQL for IRIS, unclear whether also used for the baseline (p. 20); possible memorisation of public CVEs (not discussed); dataset curated by the tool's own authors (p. 19).
154	- External (generalisability of sample/context): [I] Java/Maven only, four CWE classes, compilable libraries only (p. 7, p. 19); vulnerabilities fixed in non-Java files excluded (p. 19).
155	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [I] FDR counts unknown real bugs as false positives (acknowledged, p. 7); "detected" relies on fix-location overlap.
156	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] No tests, number of runs not reported; N=120 overall but small per-CWE cells (CWE-78 N=13).
157	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [V] Code, dataset, model IDs and hyper-parameters are reported (p. 1, p. 2, p. 20–21). [I] Pinned OpenAI model snapshots may be retired, which limits exact replication.
158	
159	## 11. Future research directions
160	- Stated by authors [A]: tighter LLM–static-analysis integration, other languages, better developer-facing reports (p. 10); dynamic approaches for CWE-78 (p. 8); probability estimates for specifications (p. 10); more source/sink kinds (p. 14).
161	- Suggested by us [I]: contamination-controlled evaluation on post-cutoff CVEs; head-to-head with LLM-only and DL detectors on CWE-Bench-Java; per-project token/dollar cost reporting.
162	
163	## 12. Relevance to our research
164	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1, RQ2, RQ3, RQ4, RQ5.
165	- How it informs our work [I]: A central hybrid study ("LLM inside SAST") with a real SAST baseline on repository-scale, real-world Java. It shows the hybrid roughly doubles recall of known CVEs over CodeQL, while precision stays poor and the gain depends on model strength. It also contributes CWE-Bench-Java, relevant to RQ2.
166	
167	## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
168	| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
169	|---|---|---|---|---|
170	| RQ1/RQ3 | IRIS+GPT-4 detects 55/120 CVEs vs CodeQL 27/120; AvgFDR 84.82% vs 90.03%; AvgF1 0.177 vs 0.076 | p. 8 | V | moderate |
171	| RQ1 | Other SAST tools on CWE-Bench-Java: Infer 0, SpotBugs 4, Snyk 23 of 120 | p. 8 | V | moderate |
172	| RQ3 | Hybrid gain depends on the LLM: only GPT-4 lowers FDR below CodeQL; L3 8B/DSC 7B FDR ~95%; LLM triage hurts small models | p. 8, p. 10 | V | moderate |
173	| RQ3 | Both LLM-inferred sources and sinks are needed (ablation 27 / 36 / 24 / 55) | p. 10 | V | moderate |
174	| RQ3 | Runtime 43 s to 4 h per project (Llama-3 8B); dollar cost not reported | p. 22–24 | V | moderate |
175	| RQ4 | Per-CWE: CWE-94 0→8, CWE-79 4→13, CWE-22 22→31, CWE-78 1→3 (hard for all tools) | p. 8 | V | moderate |
176	| RQ2 | New benchmark CWE-Bench-Java: 120 compilable, manually vetted real-world Java CVEs, avg 300K SLOC | p. 7, p. 19 | V | moderate |
177	| RQ2/RQ5 | Data contamination of public CVEs is not addressed | p. 7–10 | I | weak |
178	| RQ5 | Authors: many vulnerabilities still undetected; many LLM calls raise cost; Java only | p. 10 | A | moderate |
179	
180	## 14. Key quotes
181	> "A state-of-the-art static analysis tool CodeQL detects only 27 of these vulnerabilities whereas IRIS with GPT-4 detects 55 (+28)" (p. 1)
182	> "the reported FDR is an upper bound" (p. 7)
183	> "IRIS makes numerous calls to LLMs for specification inference and filtering false positives, increasing the potential cost of analysis." (p. 10)
184	
185	## Analyst notes
186	- Reading coverage: whole paper read (main text, appendices A–D incl. Table 10). Figures 6, 7 and 9 were read from PDF page images (p. 9–10) because their values are not in the text layer.
187	- Version: arXiv v3, 6 Apr 2025, ICLR 2025 header (p. 1). We did not have v1; earlier versions reportedly gave different numbers, so no v1 figure is cited. When other papers quote IRIS numbers, check which version they used.
188	- Venue: metadata says preprint; the text is the ICLR 2025 version. Treat as a peer-reviewed conference paper in substance, while citing the arXiv record.
189	- Uncertainties: Fig. 6/7/9 values read from bar labels in the PDF image; per-model precision/F1 before triage is only shown as deltas (Fig. 9).

229	  "abstract": "Code auditing is the process of reviewing code with the aim of identifying bugs. Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated promising capabilities for this task without requiring compilation, while also supporting user-friendly customization. However, auditing a code repository with LLMs poses significant challenges: limited context windows and hallucinations can degrade the quality of bug reports, and analyzing large-scale repositories incurs substantial time and token costs, hindering efficiency and scalability. Equipped with agent memory, RepoAudit explores the codebase on demand by analyzing data-flow facts along feasible program paths within individual functions. It further incorporates a validator module to mitigate hallucinations by verifying data-flow facts and checking the satisfiability of path conditions associated with potential bugs, thereby reducing false positives. 277	# RepoAudit: An Autonomous LLM-Agent for Repository-Level Code Auditing
278	
279	- Authors: Guo, Jinyao; Wang, Chengpeng; Xu, Xiangzhe; Su, Zian; Zhang, Xiangyu
280	- Year / venue: 2025, arXiv (preprint)
281	- DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2501.18160 · URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.18160
282	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index). Our PDF is arXiv:2501.18160v3 (29 May 2025). Its p. 1 already carries the footer "Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, Vancouver, Canada. PMLR 267, 2025" (p. 1), so it appears to be the camera-ready text, but rlab records the paper as an arXiv preprint.
283	
284	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
285	Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.
286	
287	## 1. Research objective
288	Build and evaluate an LLM agent that audits whole C/C++ repositories for path-sensitive memory bugs without compilation, overcoming context limits, hallucination and cost of direct prompting [A] (p. 1, p. 2).
289	
290	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
291	- No explicit RQs. Implicit questions: effectiveness on known bugs, comparison with LLM-based and industrial detectors, contribution of components (ablation), sensitivity to model and temperature, real-world impact [V] (p. 7, p. 8).
292	- Underlying claim: LLMs are good at function-local abstraction, pointer handling and feasible-path exploration, but poor at whole-repository reasoning [A] (p. 3, p. 4).
293	
294	## 3. Methodology
295	- Research design: design-and-evaluate tool paper with comparative experiments, ablations and a field deployment [V] (p. 7, p. 8, p. 15).
296	- Approach / model / intervention: three components [V] (p. 5–7): an initiator (tree-sitter pattern matchers find source values, e.g. NULL literals); an explorer that prompts the LLM one function at a time to derive data-flow facts along feasible paths, stores them in agent memory (also used as a cache) and moves to callers/callees on demand; a validator that checks control-flow order of data-flow facts with a parser and asks the LLM whether inter-procedural path conditions are satisfiable. Calling-context bound K = 4 functions, temperature 0.0, default model Claude 3.5 Sonnet [V] (p. 7).
297	- Baselines or comparison conditions: Meta Infer and Amazon CodeGuru (industrial static analyzers) [V] (p. 8, p. 14); single-function and multiple-function few-shot CoT prompting and the LLMDFA agent (only on functions related to RepoAudit's TPs, or reachable from sources) [V] (p. 13). No open-source SAST such as CodeQL/Semgrep/CSA, no deep-learning detectors.
298	
299	## 4. Dataset and sample
300	- Data source(s): 15 projects (5 per bug type) taken from bug reports of prior papers (Huang et al. 2024; Shi et al. 2021, 2018) [V] (p. 7). NPD: sofa-pbrpc, ImageMagick/MagickCore, coturn, libfreenect, openldap; MLK: libsass, memcached, linux/driver/net, linux/sound, linux/mm; UAF: Redis, linux/drivers/peci, shadowsocks-libev, wabt-tool, icu i18n; 2,130–1,378,262 LoC [V] (p. 7, Table 1).
301	- Sample size (N) and unit: 15 projects with 21 previously reported bugs (counted as "Old" TPs) [V] (p. 8, p. 17); 9 further projects of 14K–1.7M LoC (avg 420K LoC) for the field study [V] (p. 8).
302	- Sampling / selection method: "well-maintained" projects from prior bug reports [A] (p. 7). The paper says both "ten actively maintained repositories" (p. 2) and "nine open-source GitHub projects" (p. 8, p. 9); Table 4 lists nine [V] (p. 9).
303	- Data availability (public? link?): code at https://github.com/PurCL/RepoAudit [V] (p. 1). A labelled dataset release is not reported.
304	
305	## 5. Experimental setup
306	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: tree-sitter for parsing/call graphs; Claude 3.5 Sonnet at temperature 0; K = 4 [V] (p. 7). Additional runs with DeepSeek R1, Claude 3.7 Sonnet and OpenAI o3-mini, and temperatures 0.25–1.0 [V] (p. 16, p. 17). Infer tried in v1.2.0, v1.0.0 and v0.9.0; 2 projects failed to build and 5 crashed or were incompatible [V] (p. 15). Infer and CodeGuru reports were manually labelled TP/FP [V] (p. 14). How RepoAudit's own reports were judged TP or FP (who labelled, criteria, agreement) is not reported.
307	- Code availability: yes (p. 1).
308	
309	## 6. Evaluation metrics
310	- Metric — what it measures — why chosen: TP, FP, precision = TP/(TP+FP); "recall" is the share of the 21 previously reported bugs reproduced (p. 17); prompting rounds, input/output tokens, USD and seconds per project (p. 8). Overall recall against all bugs in the projects is not measured.
311	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): none; single run per setting (temperature study gives one run per temperature) [V] (p. 17).
312	
313	## 7. Key findings
314	1. RepoAudit (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) reproduces all 21 known bugs and finds 19 new ones (14 fixed in the latest commit): 40 TPs, 11 FPs, precision 78.43%; 21 TPs are inter-procedural — [V] (p. 7, Table 2 p. 8).
315	2. Cost: average 0.44 h (1,577.22 s), 100.67 prompts, 614,625.73 input and 46,153.07 output tokens, $2.54 per project, $0.95 per true bug; most expensive project (icu) $18.15 and 10,661.98 s — [V] (p. 7, p. 8).
316	3. Meta Infer: 13 projects build but 5 crash; on 8 analysed projects 7 TPs and 2 FPs, no MLK or UAF bug found — [V] (p. 8, p. 15). Amazon CodeGuru (NPD and UAF only, 10 projects): 0 TPs and 18 FPs — [V] (p. 8, p. 15).
317	4. LLM baselines: single-function CoT finds 1 true bug, multiple-function CoT 10; LLMDFA needs on average 165.23× (path scan) to 1,737.04× (source scan) the prompts and 123.18×–1,193.63× the input tokens of RepoAudit — [V] (p. 8, p. 14).
318	5. Ablations: without abstraction TPs −47.50%, FPs +181.82% (precision 40.38%); without validators FPs +245.45% (31 FPs); without caching ~3.5× prompts, 3.48× cost, 3.75× time, icu exceeds 72 h — [V] (p. 8, p. 15, p. 16).
319	6. Other models: DeepSeek R1 46 TPs, precision 88.46%, $0.57 but 4,571.72 s per project; Claude 3.7 Sonnet 46 TPs, 86.79%, $1.59; o3-mini 42 TPs, 82.35%, $0.30, ~625 s — [V] (p. 8, p. 16, p. 17).
320	7. Temperature 0–1.0: precision 72.92–78.43%, recall of known bugs 85.71–100% — [V] (p. 17, Table 11).
321	8. Field study on 9 projects: 185 new bugs reported at 85.71% precision; 95 confirmed and 79 fixed (174 total); libuv (86 NPD) and memcached (67 MLK) dominate — [V] (p. 8, p. 9, Table 4).
322	9. 19 of 25 CWE Top-25 (2024) weaknesses need global path-sensitive reasoning — [A] (p. 3).
323	
324	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
325	- [A] FPs and FNs from LLM hallucination (p. 9).
326	- [A] Cost is highly sensitive to the number of source elements in a repository (p. 9).
327	- [A] Not sound inter-procedurally: limited to four functions, may miss bugs with longer call chains (p. 9).
328	- [A] FP example: unaware of external (YANG schema) constraints; FN example: Claude 3.5 Sonnet missed an error-handling path (p. 18).
329	- [A] Possible leakage of private source code to LLM providers and token costs (p. 10).
330	
331	## 9. Limitations we identified
332	- [I] Evaluation by the tool's own authors; the TP/FP judgement procedure for RepoAudit's reports is not described, while Infer/CodeGuru reports were "manually" checked (p. 14). Based on p. 7–8, p. 14.
333	- [I] Recall is only measured on 21 previously reported bugs (one per project for most), so true recall is unknown; FNs beyond these are not counted. Based on Table 2 (p. 8) and Table 11 (p. 17).
334	- [I] Industrial baselines are disadvantaged by build failures and crashes (Infer analysed only 8/15 projects); no compile-free open-source SAST (Semgrep, CodeQL build-less modes) or CSA baseline. Based on p. 15.
335	- [I] Benchmark projects come from prior papers' public bug reports, so model memorisation of known bugs cannot be excluded; not discussed. Based on p. 7.
336	- [I] Internal inconsistencies: "ten" (p. 2) vs "nine" (p. 8, p. 9) field-study repositories; Table 4 MLK TP column sums to 75 while the printed total is 76 (NPD 107 + MLK 75 + UAF 3 = 185, matching the text; the 85.71% precision matches 186/217). Based on Table 4 (p. 9).
337	- [I] Documented tension with the later independent evaluation in li2026llm. Both sides are confirmed in the texts, but li is not a replication on the same bugs. Based on the pages cited below.
338	  - Effectiveness. guo: all 21 previously reported bugs are reproduced and 19 new ones found, for 40 TPs / 11 FPs and a precision of 78.43% on 15 C/C++ projects (p. 7, Table 2 p. 8). li: RepoAudit (Sonnet 3.5) detects 0 of 110 and RepoAudit (GPT-5.4) 2 of 110 known C/C++ vulnerabilities [@li2026llm, p. 7]. Its real-world SFDR is 92.77%, a 9-project average [@li2026llm, p. 11].
339	  - Dataset. guo's "Old" bugs are bug reports from prior tools/papers (p. 7; Table 2 caption, p. 8). li's 0/110 comes from its *controlled* ReposVul set. That set uses "the three repositories with the most cases" per CWE, and li does not name them [@li2026llm, p. 5]. The shared targets are linux/sound, linux/mm, linux/drivers/net, linux/drivers/peci and ImageMagick (Table 1, p. 7; [@li2026llm, p. 6]). They appear only in li's *real-world* set, where recall is not measured. For 3 of the 5 the bug type differs:
340	    - ImageMagick: NPD here, CWE-401 in li.
341	    - linux/driver/net: MLK here, CWE-416 in li.
342	    - peci: UAF here, CWE-476 in li.
343	
344	    The sizes differ at every shared target (here vs li): linux/sound 1,378,262 vs 1,253,234; linux/mm 171,721 vs 133,952; peci 2,130 vs 1,715; ImageMagick/MagickCore 242,555 vs the whole ImageMagick repository at 680,878. guo's "linux/driver/net" (914,025 LoC) is closer in size to li's linux/net (962,143) than to li's linux/drivers/net (3,924,621), so it is unclear which li module it corresponds to. Both li modules are CWE-416, and on linux/net RepoAudit emits 3 warnings with an SFDR of 66.67% [@li2026llm, p. 6, p. 11]. On the other shared projects li's RepoAudit (Sonnet 3.5) emits 0 warnings (linux/sound, linux/mm, ImageMagick), 1 warning (linux/drivers/net, an FP) and 3 warnings (peci, all FPs) [@li2026llm, p. 11].
345	  - Commit. guo analyses the versions used by the earlier works. Its new bugs are found "in historic versions", 14 of them fixed in the latest commit (p. 7, p. 8). li uses recent commits: 6093a68 for Linux and 3bf1076 for ImageMagick [@li2026llm, p. 6]. guo's 4 Linux known bugs are all intra-procedural (Table 2, p. 8), as li also notes [@li2026llm, p. 7].
346	  - Metric. guo reports precision on the tool's own reports plus reproduction of 21 known bugs (p. 17). li reports recall on CVEs and SFDR [@li2026llm, p. 6].
347	  - Labeller. guo does not describe how RepoAudit's reports were judged; only the Infer/CodeGuru reports are said to be checked manually (p. 14). li labels warnings with Codex and validates manually [@li2026llm, p. 11].
348	  - Explanation (ours). Target selection, code version, bug-type mapping, scale, metric and labeller all differ, so the results are not directly comparable. li records 0.00 input tokens for RepoAudit on at least one project [@li2026llm, p. 16] and attributes all 108/108 misses of RepoAudit (GPT-5.4) to incomplete API modelling / candidate exploration [@li2026llm, p. 7]. guo's own Linux runs used only 1–35 prompts each (Table 2, p. 8). Together these point to source/sink coverage as one plausible mechanism.
349	- [I] Cost contradiction with li2026llm. guo reports an average of $2.54 and 0.44 h per project, with a maximum of $18.15 and 10,661.98 s on icu (p. 7, Table 2 p. 8). li measures RepoAudit (Sonnet 3.5) at an average of $172.77 and a maximum of $1,247.66 per project, with a maximum runtime over 800 min [@li2026llm, p. 15, p. 16]. The projects and their sizes differ:
350	  - guo's projects average 251 KLoC, and its Linux modules cost $0.03–$0.86 (p. 7, p. 8).
351	  - li analyses modules of up to 3,924,621 LOC plus gpac and bitlbee, with no budget or timeout limits [@li2026llm, p. 6]. Which project cost the most in li is not reported in li's main text.
352	  - guo itself says cost depends on the number of source elements (p. 9).
353	
354	  guo's per-project cost therefore should not be generalised to large repositories.
355	- [I] "Bugs" (NPD/MLK/UAF) are memory-safety defects, not necessarily exploitable vulnerabilities.
356	
357	## 10. Threats to validity
358	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): author-evaluated; labelling procedure not reported; possible pretraining exposure to known bugs; baselines restricted to RepoAudit-related functions in the LLM comparison (p. 13).
359	- External (generalisability of sample/context): C/C++ only, 3 bug types, 15 + 9 projects (p. 7, p. 9).
360	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): "recall" = reproduction of 21 known bugs, not overall recall (p. 17).
361	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): no tests; one run per configuration; small counts (11 FPs).
362	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): code public (p. 1); prompts partly shown (p. 6, p. 7); full labelled report set not reported.
363	
364	## 11. Future research directions
365	- Stated by authors [A]: stronger or fine-tuned models for sub-tasks such as feasible-path exploration (p. 9); a richer compilation-free tool suite to expose branches/loops to the model (p. 9); extension to other languages (Python, JavaScript) (p. 10).
366	- Suggested by us [I]: independent replication with blinded labelling and recall on unseen, post-cutoff bugs; comparison with build-free SAST (Semgrep) and CSA on identical targets.
367	
368	## 12. Relevance to our research
369	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1, RQ3, RQ4, RQ5.
370	- How it informs our work [I]: a representative agentic LLM detector with explicit cost data and a direct comparison with industrial static analyzers (Infer, CodeGuru). Its strong self-reported precision and low cost vs li2026llm's independent evaluation (on different targets, commits and metrics; see §9) is a key tension for RQ1/RQ2/RQ3 and illustrates how evaluation setup drives reported results.
371	
372	## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
373	| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
374	|---|---|---|---|---|
375	| RQ1 | RepoAudit (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) finds 40 TPs / 11 FPs (precision 78.43%) on 15 C/C++ projects for NPD/MLK/UAF | p. 7, p. 8 | V | weak |
376	| RQ1 | Meta Infer finds 7 TPs / 2 FPs on the 8 projects it could analyse; Amazon CodeGuru 0 TPs / 18 FPs | p. 8, p. 15 | V | weak |
377	| RQ1 | With reasoning models RepoAudit precision rises to 82.35–88.46% (42–46 TPs) | p. 8, p. 16 | V | weak |
378	| RQ2 | Recall is measured only as reproduction of 21 previously reported bugs; overall recall unknown | p. 17 | V | moderate |
379	| RQ3 | Average cost $2.54, 0.44 h and ~615K input tokens per project; $0.95 per true bug; o3-mini $0.30, DeepSeek R1 $0.57 | p. 7, p. 8, p. 16, p. 17 | V | moderate |
380	| RQ3 | Cost contradiction: li2026llm measures RepoAudit (Sonnet 3.5) at avg $172.77, max $1,247.66 and >800 min per project vs $2.54 / 0.44 h here; different projects and sizes (avg 251 KLoC here vs Linux modules up to 3.9M LOC, gpac, bitlbee in li) | p. 7, p. 8 | I | weak |
381	| RQ2 | Tension with li2026llm (0/110 known C/C++ vulns, 92.77% SFDR): overlapping projects only in li's real-world set, at newer commits and partly different bug types; precision vs recall/SFDR; different labellers (see §9) | p. 7, p. 8 | I | weak |
382	| RQ3 | Validator removal raises FPs by 245.45%; abstraction removal cuts TPs by 47.50% and raises FPs by 181.82% | p. 8, p. 15 | V | weak |
383	| RQ3 | Compilation-dependent analyzers fail on some projects (2 build failures, 5 Infer crashes of 15); RepoAudit needs no build | p. 15 | V | moderate |
384	| RQ4 | Evaluated only on C/C++ memory bugs (CWE-476/401/416); call-chain depth limited to 4 functions | p. 7, p. 9 | V | moderate |
385	| RQ5 | Field study: 185 new bugs in 9 projects, 174 confirmed or fixed | p. 8, p. 9 | A | weak |
386

388	> "In total, it reports 40 TPs and 11 FPs, resulting in a precision of 78.43%." (p. 7)
389

391
