87	# Reducing False Positives in Static Bug Detection with LLMs: An Empirical Study in Industry
88	
89	- Authors: Du, Xueying; Feng, Jiayi; Zou, Yi; Xu, Wei; Ma, Jie; Zhang, Wei; Liu, Sisi; Peng, Xin; Lou, Yiling
90	- Year / venue: 2026, Proceedings of the IEEE/ACM 48th International Conference on Software Engineering: Software Engineering in Practice (published)
91	- DOI: 10.1145/3786583.3786910 · URL: https://doi.org/10.1145/3786583.3786910
92	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)
93	
94	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
95	Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.
96	
97	**Version note:** our text is arXiv 2601.18844 **v1 (26 Jan 2026)** in a generic ACM template ("Conference'17, July 2017, Washington, DC, USA" running header, p. 2). It is not the ICSE-SEIP 2026 camera-ready recorded in metadata; final numbers may differ.
98	
99	**Scope note:** the bug types are **general static-analysis bug classes, not classic security-vulnerability classes**: Null Pointer Dereference (NPD), Out-of-Bounds (OOB) and Divide-by-Zero (DBZ), reported by Tencent's quality-oriented SAT BkCheck (p. 2, p. 4). The paper itself calls them "memory safety bugs" (p. 10) and does not map them to CWEs or rate exploitability. [I] They overlap with CWE-476 / CWE-125/787 / CWE-369, so the study is indirect evidence for security-vulnerability triage; weight it accordingly.
100	
101	## 1. Research objective
102	- [A] Find out how well LLM-based false-alarm reduction techniques work on real proprietary enterprise code and an enterprise-customised static analyser, since earlier work used open-source or synthetic benchmarks (p. 1–2).
103	
104	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
105	- [V] RQ1: prevalence of false positives in industrial practice; RQ2: effectiveness of LLM-based techniques (2.a plain LLMs, 2.b advanced prompting, 2.c hybrid LLM + static analysis, 2.d vs traditional learning-based methods); RQ3: time and money costs; RQ4: per-bug-type breakdown and failure-case analysis (p. 4–6).
106	
107	## 3. Methodology
108	- Research design: [V] Industrial empirical study: developer interviews (RQ1) plus offline evaluation of LLM and DL techniques on a labelled set of historical alarms (RQ2–RQ4) (p. 4–6).
109	- Approach / model / intervention: [V] LLMs: GPT-4o, Claude-Opus-4, Qwen-3-Coder, DeepSeek-R1 (p. 5). Prompting: basic, Chain-of-Thought, few-shot, bug-type augmentation (p. 5). Hybrid LLM + static analysis: LLM4SA (LLM sees the warning plus callers/callees and hundreds of lines of context) and LLM4PFA (static-analysis path constraints plus agent-driven feasibility reasoning) (p. 5). [V] IRIS and LLMDFA were excluded: IRIS needs a compilable repository for CodeQL, LLMDFA does not support the bug types (p. 5).
110	- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] The SAT alone (all alarms reported); DL methods Devign, ReGVD (GNN), LLMAO, LineVul (fine-tuned PLMs), applied with models trained on their original datasets, without retraining (p. 5–6).
111	
112	## 4. Dataset and sample
113	- Data source(s): [V] Alarms from BkCheck, Tencent's proprietary SAT (no compilation needed; rules include null dereference, logic defects, divide-by-zero, memory leaks), on the Advertising and Marketing Services (AMS) repositories, Sep 2024–Jun 2025; labels from Tencent's two-round routine code review (p. 3–4). [A] Data are "primarily" C/C++ (p. 10).
114	- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] 433 alarms: NPD 136 (107 FP / 29 TP), DBZ 158 (139 / 19), OOB 139 (82 / 57); total 328 FP / 105 TP (Table 1, p. 4). [V] Interviews: 5 participants (2 developers, 3 reviewers, >5 years' experience) (p. 4).
115	- Sampling / selection method: [V] All records of the three most frequent categories (≈52%, 24%, 10% of warnings, 86% total) in the period, minus deprecated code, incomplete context, unresolved cases and duplicates (p. 4). How many records were removed: not reported.
116	- Data availability (public? link?): [V] Dataset not released (confidentiality); methods and detailed results in a replication package at https://github.com/LLM4SFPR/static-bug-false-positives-reduction-in-practice (p. 2, p. 11).
117	
118	## 5. Experimental setup
119	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] Each LLM query run three times per case with majority vote (p. 6). DL models used as trained on their original datasets (p. 6). Temperature, prompt texts, few-shot example source and context lengths: not reported in the paper (prompts said to be in the replication package, p. 5). [V] IRB approval for the interviews (p. 4).
120	- Code availability: [V] Replication package (p. 2, p. 11).
121	
122	## 6. Evaluation metrics
123	- [V] Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 with the real bug as positive class; FPR_P = TN/(TN+FN) and FPR_R = TN/(TN+FP), i.e., precision and recall on false alarms (FPR_R = share of false alarms removed) (p. 6).
124	- [V] Cost: average response time (s) and API cost (USD) per alarm (p. 5–6, p. 8).
125	- Statistical testing: not reported (no significance tests, CIs or variance across the three runs).
126	
127	## 7. Key findings
128	1. [V] SAT alone: 76% of alarms in the final dataset are false (328/433) (p. 6). [A] Counting excluded records, the false-positive rate exceeds 90% (p. 6); how this was computed is not reported.
129	2. [A] Interviews: every alarm is manually reviewed, false alarms get a second review; about 10 minutes per round, 10–20 minutes per alarm (p. 6).
130	3. [V] Hybrid LLM4PFA: accuracy 0.93–0.94, precision 0.83–0.93, recall 0.75–0.88, F1 0.83–0.86, FPR_R 0.94–0.98 across the four LLMs (e.g., GPT-4o: P 0.93, R 0.75, FPR_R 0.98; Claude-Opus-4: P 0.83, R 0.88, FPR_R 0.94) (Table 2, p. 8).
131	4. [V] Hybrid LLM4SA: accuracy 0.86–0.92, recall 0.65–0.86, FPR_R 0.84–0.96 (Table 2, p. 8).
132	5. [V] Prompting-only LLMs are much weaker: basic prompt accuracy 0.40–0.55, precision 0.26–0.29, FPR_R 0.26–0.52; few-shot is the best prompting strategy (accuracy 0.50–0.72, FPR_R 0.43–0.72); CoT is weakest (FPR_R 0.24–0.40) (Table 2, p. 8).
133	6. [V] DL baselines: Devign accuracy 0.44, ReGVD 0.36 (recall 0.87 but FPR_R 0.19), LLMAO 0.36, LineVul 0.76 only because it labels every alarm a false positive (precision/recall 0.00) (Table 3, p. 8; p. 7).
134	7. [V] Cost per alarm, LLM4PFA: 12.6–58.3 s and $0.0025–$0.12 (Claude-Opus-4 most expensive); overall range for all LLM methods 2.1–109.5 s and $0.0011–$0.12 (Table 4, p. 8). Cost per project or per scan: not reported.
135	8. [V] By bug type, most methods do best on DBZ and worst on NPD (p. 8; Fig. 3, p. 9).
136	9. [V] Failure cases: functions in all-methods-failed cases are 95.6 lines longer than the dataset average and contain 21 more conditional statements (p. 9).
137	10. [A] LLM explanations cut the time to validate a warning from about 10 to about 3 minutes (p. 10); how this was measured is not reported.
138	
139	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
140	- [A] Recall stays below the 90% enterprise threshold, so manual review is still needed; LLMs can replace at least one review round (p. 9).
141	- [A] Long-context and complex cascaded-constraint reasoning remain weak; strong results partly reflect short code fragments in this analyser's warnings (p. 9–10).
142	- [A] Study focuses on memory-safety bugs; other bug types are an open question (p. 10).
143	- [A] LLM randomness; majority voting recommended (p. 10).
144	- [A] LLMs can only filter, not find bugs beyond the analyser's coverage (p. 10).
145	- [A] Label reliability, limited dataset scope (433 cases, 10 months), and one company, mostly C/C++ (p. 10).
146	
147	## 9. Limitations we identified
148	- [I] Conflict of interest: LLM4PFA, the winning method, is the authors' own earlier work (ref [15], same first and last authors, p. 3, p. 11), and the dataset is private, so the result cannot be checked independently.
149	- [I] Industry conflict of interest: four of the nine authors (Wei Xu, Jie Ma, Wei Zhang, Sisi Liu) are Tencent employees with Tencent addresses (p. 1), and the study evaluates Tencent's own analyser (BkCheck) on Tencent data (p. 1–2). Funding: not reported (no acknowledgements section found). Based on the author affiliations and contact list on p. 1.
150	- [I] Bug classes are reliability/memory-safety bugs from a quality-oriented analyser, not security vulnerabilities from a SAST tool; transfer to RQ1–RQ4 on vulnerabilities is indirect.
151	- [I] The DL comparison is unfair: Devign, ReGVD, LineVul are function-level vulnerability detectors (and LLMAO a fault localiser) used without retraining on alarm triage; poor results show domain shift, not that DL triage cannot work.
152	- [I] Model identity is unclear: references cite Claude 3.5 Sonnet for "Claude-Opus-4" [8], DeepSeek-Coder-V2 for "DeepSeek-R1" [13], GPT-4 Turbo for "GPT-4o" [21] and Qwen2.5-Coder-32B for "Qwen-3-Coder" [45] (p. 11–12).
153	- [I] Prompting-only precision (0.26–0.29) is barely above the base rate of real bugs (105/433 ≈ 0.24, our arithmetic from Table 1), so plain LLMs add little signal here.
154	- [I] Few-shot examples were "manually constructed" (p. 10); whether they came from the evaluation set is not reported, so leakage cannot be ruled out.
155	- [I] The ">90%" false-positive figure and the "10 → 3 minutes" saving lack described measurement.
156	- [I] The text is the v1 preprint, not the peer-reviewed camera-ready.
157	
158	## 10. Threats to validity
159	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [I] Author-built method wins; filtering of records with incomplete context may remove the hardest cases; possible few-shot leakage.
160	- External (generalisability of sample/context): [I] One company, one business line, one proprietary analyser, three bug types, mostly C/C++ (p. 4, p. 10).
161	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [I] Labels come from routine review (p. 4); the authors argue true positives are unlikely to be discarded (p. 4), but this is not tested.
162	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] N=433 with only 105 TPs (19 for DBZ); no tests; differences of 0.01–0.02 between LLM4PFA backbones are within noise.
163	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [V] Code and results public, data confidential (p. 2). [I] Cannot be replicated on the same data.
164	
165	## 11. Future research directions
166	- Stated by authors [A]: knowledge-enhanced LLMs (e.g., RAG of historical cases); decomposing complex constraint reasoning and hybrid pipelines for long context (p. 10); using LLMs to find bugs beyond analyser coverage (p. 10); more business lines and languages (p. 10).
167	- Suggested by us [I]: replicate on security-relevant SAST alerts (CWE-tagged) and on public industrial-like data; independent evaluation of LLM4PFA.
168	
169	## 12. Relevance to our research
170	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1, RQ3, RQ4, RQ5.
171	- How it informs our work [I]: Real-world industrial evidence that hybrid static analysis + LLM post-filtering beats prompting-only LLMs and off-the-shelf DL detectors for alarm triage, with per-alarm cost. Relevance is medium rather than high because the bugs are general static bugs, not security vulnerabilities, and the data are private.
172	
173	## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
174	| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
175	|---|---|---|---|---|
176	| RQ1/RQ3 | Industrial SAT alone: 76% of alarms false (328/433); hybrid LLM4PFA removes 94–98% of false alarms, keeping 75–88% of real bugs (precision 0.83–0.93) | p. 6, p. 8 | V | moderate |
177	| RQ3 | Hybrid (LLM4SA, LLM4PFA; accuracy 0.86–0.94) beats prompting-only LLMs (accuracy 0.40–0.72) on the same alarms | p. 8 | V | moderate |
178	| RQ1 | Off-the-shelf DL detectors (Devign, ReGVD, LLMAO, LineVul) fail at alarm triage (accuracy 0.36–0.44; LineVul labels all as FP) | p. 7–8 | V | weak |
179	| RQ3 | Cost per alarm: LLM4PFA 12.6–58.3 s, $0.0025–$0.12; all LLM methods 2.1–109.5 s, $0.0011–$0.12 vs 10–20 min manual | p. 6, p. 8 | V | moderate |
180	| RQ4 | Best on Divide-by-Zero, worst on Null Pointer Dereference; failures tied to long functions and many conditionals | p. 8–9 | V | weak |
181	| RQ5 | Recall below 90% enterprise threshold; LLMs can only filter, not find bugs beyond analyser coverage | p. 9–10 | A | moderate |
182	| RQ2 | Scope: general bug classes (NPD/OOB/DBZ), proprietary C/C++ data, author-built winning method | p. 4, p. 10 | I | weak |
183	
184	## 14. Key quotes
185	> "hybrid techniques of LLM and static analysis eliminate 94–98% of false positives with high recall" (p. 1)
186	> "recall remains below the enterprise-expected threshold of 90%, indicating that some degree of manual review is still necessary" (p. 9)
187	> "their capacity to discover new bugs remains bounded by the detection capabilities of static analyzers themselves" (p. 10)
188

190	- Reading coverage: whole paper read (pp. 1–10 text, pp. 11–12 references). Fig. 3 (per-bug-type bars, p. 9) is garbled in the text layer; only the prose summary of it is cited.

192	- Uncertainties: exact model versions (reference mismatch, see §9); number of records removed by filtering; temperature and prompt content not in the paper.

251	# Sifting the Noise: A Comparative Study of LLM Agents in Vulnerability False Positive Filtering
252	
253	- Authors: Xiong, Yunpeng; Zhang, Ting
254	- Year / venue: 2026, Proceedings of the ACM on Software Engineering (published)
255	- DOI: 10.1145/3832100 · URL: https://doi.org/10.1145/3832100
256	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)
257	
258	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
259	Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.
260	
261	**Version note:** our text is arXiv 2601.22952 **v3 (23 Jul 2026)**, formatted as the PACMSE ISSTA 2026 article (ISSTA009) with "Received 2026-01-30; accepted 2026-06-25" (p. 1, p. 24). It matches the DOI in metadata.
262	
263	## 1. Research objective
264	- [A] Compare LLM-based agent frameworks (Aider, OpenHands, SWE-agent) for filtering false positives (FPs) produced by SAST tools, and find out whether agentic reasoning beats vanilla one-shot LLM prompting and at what cost (p. 1–2).
265	
266	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
267	- [V] RQ1: effectiveness of agent frameworks in filtering SAST FPs (OWASP Benchmark); RQ2: effectiveness on real-world Java (Vul4J/CodeQL); RQ3: which agentic capabilities drive performance and whether gains generalise to a contamination-free C/C++ setting; RQ4: success drivers and failure modes (p. 6).
268	
269	## 3. Methodology
270	- Research design: [V] Comparative empirical study: 3 agents × 3 backbone LLMs plus vanilla zero-shot prompting, on a synthetic benchmark and real-world alerts, followed by ablations, stronger baselines and qualitative trajectory analysis (p. 2–3, p. 6–10).
271	- Approach / model / intervention: [V] Each agent gets the SAST warning(s) for the target file, code access, and a prompt to "verify if this static analysis finding represents a real vulnerability or an FP"; browser/web tools disabled where possible (p. 7). Backbones: Claude Sonnet 4 (claude-sonnet-4-20250514), DeepSeek Chat (deepseek-chat), GPT-5 (gpt-5-2025-08-07) (p. 7).
272	- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] SAST tools alone (CodeQL v2.23.7, Semgrep v1.145.0, SonarQube Community v9.9.8, Joern v4.0.454, default rules) (p. 6); vanilla zero-shot LLM with repo structure + flagged file + findings (p. 7). [V] On OSS-Fuzz also: LLM4SA-style prompt (without LLM4SA's program-dependence context extraction), context-augmented vanilla LLM, oracle-context vanilla LLM (same files the agent opened), and four ablations (no multi-turn, no cross-file navigation, no tool-based verification, no config-file access) (p. 10). No deep-learning FP classifier baseline.
273	
274	## 4. Dataset and sample
275	- Data source(s): [V] OWASP Benchmark for Java v1.2 (synthetic servlets with injected vulnerabilities, labelled) (p. 6); Vul4J (79 reproducible Java vulnerabilities from Project KB, 25 CWEs) (p. 8); OSS-Fuzz/OSV records for 5 C/C++ projects (mpv, libhevc, libical, gpsd, quickjs) with fixing commits 10–12 months after Claude Sonnet 4's training cutoff (p. 9).
276	- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] OWASP: 2,740 test cases, 1,415 vulnerable / 1,325 non-vulnerable, 11 CWEs (Table 1, p. 6). [V] Vul4J: 79 versions, 6,786,406 SLOC, 3,426 CodeQL alerts, of which 50 alerts were sampled (26 projects, 16 CodeQL rules), labelled 31 FP / 19 TP (p. 8–9). [V] OSS-Fuzz: 804 eligible CodeQL alerts, 50 sampled (seed 42), 11 rule IDs, labelled 22 FP / 28 TP (p. 9–10). [V] RQ4: 256 success and 103 failure trajectories inspected (p. 10).
277	- Sampling / selection method: [V] OWASP: candidate set = union of instances flagged by ≥1 SAST tool (p. 7). Vul4J and OSS-Fuzz: random sampling with fixed seed (p. 8, p. 9).
278	- Data availability (public? link?): [V] Scripts and data stated to be public at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18420284 (p. 21). [I] The reference list gives a different Zenodo DOI for the same artifact (10.5281/zenodo.21282004, ref [6], p. 21); which is current is unclear.
279	
280	## 5. Experimental setup
281	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] Aider v0.86.1, OpenHands Agent SDK v1.5.2, SWE-agent commit 1d3cfb (p. 7). [V] Temperature 0 (p. 19). [V] Browser-access check on 50 OWASP cases with OpenHands+Claude: 86.0% FP identification with browser disabled vs 82.0% enabled (p. 7). [V] Vul4J ground truth: method-level patch matching (2 TPs) plus manual labelling of 48 alerts by the first author (6 years' experience), about 20 person-hours (p. 8–9). [V] OSS-Fuzz ground truth: two independent raters, 86.0% raw agreement, Cohen's κ = 0.725, disagreements resolved by discussion (p. 10). Number of runs per case: not reported (appears to be one).
282	- Code availability: [V] Zenodo artifact (p. 21).
283	
284	## 6. Evaluation metrics
285	- [V] RQ1 FPR: share of non-vulnerable instances flagged positive; after filtering, the remaining FPR (p. 7, p. 12).
286	- [V] RQ2/RQ3: alert-level binary classification with SAST FPs as the positive class: Identified FP, Missed FP, Mis-identified FP (true vulnerability wrongly filtered, a "safety violation"), Correct Retention; recall = FP identification rate, precision = share of alerts called FP that truly are FP, F1, accuracy (p. 9, p. 10).
287	- [V] TP retention / miss rate on OWASP positives (p. 18). Cost: average rounds, tokens and USD per task (p. 17).
288	- Statistical testing: not reported. [I] The abstract says agents "significantly outperform" vanilla prompting (p. 1), but no significance test is reported; Cohen's κ is the only statistic.
289	
290	## 7. Key findings
291	1. [V] SAST alone on OWASP: CodeQL precision 60.3%, recall 97.0%, F1 74.4%, FPR 68.2% (904 FPs); Semgrep precision 56.3%, recall 90.4%, FPR 74.8%; SonarQube precision 51.9%, recall 95.6%, FPR 94.6% (1,254 FPs); Joern precision 54.7%, recall 8.2%, FPR 7.2% (Table 2, p. 10–11).
292	2. [V] FPs are largely shared across tools: 36 FP instances flagged by all four tools; CodeQL, Semgrep and SonarQube jointly flag 710 (p. 11).
293	3. [V] The union of tools flags 1,303 of 1,325 non-vulnerable cases (98.3% FPR); after agent filtering the remaining FPR is 6.3% (SWE-agent+Claude), 14.3% (Aider+Claude), 14.9% (OpenHands+Claude), vs 23.0% for vanilla Claude; DeepSeek: vanilla 11.2% is best, agents 13.1–15.8%; GPT-5: vanilla 20.4%, agents 14.1–20.3% (Table 3, p. 12).
294	4. [V] TP retention (SWE-agent+Claude, OWASP positives): 314 of 1,411 completed runs wrongly labelled FP; retention 77.7%, miss rate 22.25%. Miss rate is ≤2.38% for CWE-78/89/79/90/643 but 77.17% CWE-327, 84.50% CWE-328, 77.11% CWE-501, 50.00% CWE-614 (p. 18).
295	5. [V] Vul4J (50 CodeQL alerts, 62% FP): best F1 83.3% (GPT-5+Aider: recall 92.6%, precision 75.8%); highest FP recall 93.3% (GPT-5+OpenHands, precision 70.0%); OpenHands+DeepSeek precision 100%, recall 38.7%; Claude agents beat vanilla Claude (F1 80.7% Aider vs 69.1%) (Table 4, p. 13–14).
296	6. [I] Derived from Table 4 (p. 13): row percentages imply some runs did not complete (e.g., GPT-5+Aider ≈ 41 scored alerts). For all four GPT-5 settings (incl. vanilla), Mis-identified FP (19.0–25.0% of alerts) against Correct Retention (12.5–21.3%) means about half to two-thirds (≈47–67%) of the true vulnerabilities in the scored sample were filtered out. The authors discuss mis-identification qualitatively (p. 14: for GPT-5 "the primary differentiator shifts to how effectively the framework avoids mis-identifying true vulnerabilities") but do not report it as a share of true vulnerabilities lost.
297	7. [V] OSS-Fuzz C/C++ (post-cutoff, Claude Sonnet 4): full SWE-agent accuracy 96.0%, precision 95.5%, recall 95.5%, F1 95.5%; vanilla recall 36.4%, F1 51.6%; LLM4SA-style F1 70.8%; context-augmented F1 66.7%; oracle-context F1 51.6%. Ablations: without cross-file navigation F1 62.5%, without multi-turn 56.3%, without tool verification 88.9%, without config read 97.7% (Table 5, p. 15).
298	8. [A] The agentic gain comes from iterative evidence gathering, not context volume, because the oracle-context baseline equals vanilla (p. 15).
299	9. [V] Cost per task (OWASP): from $0.0028 (Aider+DeepSeek, 11,036 tokens) to $0.1867 (OpenHands+Claude, 20.5 rounds, 219,299 tokens); SWE-agent+Claude $0.1501, 130,846 tokens (Table 8, p. 17).
300	10. [V] Contamination checks: filename-only probe stays at chance (49.8–51.6% accuracy); no trajectory among 15,636 claims prior exposure (p. 18).
301	11. [V] Weaker-backbone "scope drift": in 145 cases DeepSeek+SWE-agent turned a correct vanilla FP verdict into TP, reporting other issues (stack traces, cookies, CRLF) instead of the alerted CWE (p. 18–19).
302	12. [V] Failure modes: incorrect CWE attribution, overly conservative threat modelling, surface-level pattern matching; concentrated in CWE-327 (85 trajectories) and CWE-614 (24) (Table 7, p. 15–17).
303	
304	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
305	- [A] LLM non-determinism; temperature 0 helps but does not guarantee determinism (p. 19).
306	- [A] Vul4J uses only 50 alerts, mostly labelled by the first author; the sample may not represent the full alert distribution or rule mix (p. 20).
307	- [A] OSS-Fuzz is a focused 50-alert validation set, not a full C/C++ benchmark, and does not rank all agents/models (p. 20).
308	- [A] Alert-specific labels count an agent wrong when it rejects the alert's rationale but finds a different real issue (p. 20).
309	- [A] Real-world evaluation mainly uses CodeQL alerts (p. 20).
310	- [A] Agents should not be used for automatic suppression; they suit decision support (p. 19).
311	
312	## 9. Limitations we identified
313	- [I] Numbers are inconsistent: the abstract says an initial FP rate of "over 92%" (p. 1), while the results give 98.3% (p. 12). The "↓" values in Table 3 (e.g., 92.1%) look like percentage-point drops, while Lesson 1 calls them "eliminating more than 92% of FPs" (p. 19); relative reduction would be about 93.6% [our arithmetic from 98.3% → 6.3%].
314	- [I] OWASP is synthetic (single-file servlets with injected flaws, p. 6), and RQ1 filters only negatives, with TP retention measured for one configuration only (p. 18). Without a full confusion matrix per configuration, precision/recall of the hybrid pipeline on OWASP cannot be compared across agents.
315	- [I] Real-world Java (N=50) and C/C++ (N=50) samples are small; per-cell differences of a few alerts change the percentages a lot, and no confidence intervals are given.
316	- [I] Incomplete runs are dropped silently in Table 4 (denominators below 50), which can bias comparisons between configurations.
317	- [I] No deep-learning or classical ML FP-classifier baseline, so LLM vs DL cannot be compared here (RQ1).
318	- [I] The OWASP filename-only probe tests label memorisation, not whether the models know OWASP code patterns; the post-cutoff C/C++ check addresses this better, but only for one configuration.
319	- [I] Ablation "w/o config read" scores higher than the full agent (F1 97.7% vs 95.5%, p. 15), which shows noise of about one alert at N=50.
320	
321	## 10. Threats to validity
322	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [I] Single annotator for most Vul4J labels (p. 20); dropped runs; possible prior exposure of models to OWASP and Vul4J (partly probed, p. 18).
323	- External (generalisability of sample/context): [I] Mostly Java; synthetic benchmark for the main comparison; C/C++ only for the best configuration and 5 projects (p. 20).
324	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [I] RQ1 "remaining FPR" ignores true-vulnerability loss unless read with Section 5.2; alert-specific labels (acknowledged, p. 20).
325	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] No tests, many configurations compared, small real-world N, apparently single runs.
326	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [V] Tool versions, model IDs and artifact are given (p. 6–7, p. 21). [I] Two different Zenodo DOIs are listed.
327	
328	## 11. Future research directions
329	- Stated by authors [A]: CWE-aware, cost-adaptive agent strategies; human-in-the-loop auditing to keep TPs; more languages and SAST tools (p. 20). Lightweight execution-based checks (p. 16).
330	- Suggested by us [I]: full confusion-matrix reporting per configuration on real-world code; larger, multi-rater real-world alert sets; comparison with DL FP classifiers.
331	
332	## 12. Relevance to our research
333	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1, RQ2, RQ3, RQ4, RQ5.
334	- How it informs our work [I]: Strong evidence for RQ3 (SAST + LLM-agent post-filtering), with explicit cost per alert and a measured TP-suppression risk. Per-CWE results (injection filtered well; crypto/policy CWEs poorly) feed RQ4. SAST-alone figures on OWASP give a clean baseline for RQ1. The post-cutoff C/C++ set is a rare contamination control for RQ2.
335	
336	## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
337	| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
338	|---|---|---|---|---|
339	| RQ1 | SAST alone on OWASP v1.2: CodeQL P 60.3% R 97.0% FPR 68.2%; Semgrep FPR 74.8%; SonarQube FPR 94.6%; Joern R 8.2% | p. 11 | V | moderate |
340	| RQ3 | Agent post-filtering cuts union-of-SAST FPR 98.3% → 6.3% (SWE-agent+Claude Sonnet 4) vs 23.0% vanilla Claude | p. 12 | V | moderate |
341	| RQ3 | Same best config wrongly filters 22.25% of true vulnerabilities (314/1,411) | p. 18 | V | moderate |
342	| RQ3 | Agent benefit is backbone-dependent: DeepSeek vanilla (11.2%) beats its agents (13.1–15.8%) | p. 12 | V | moderate |
343	| RQ3 | Cost per alert $0.0028–$0.1867, 11k–269k tokens depending on agent/model | p. 17 | V | moderate |
344	| RQ1/RQ3 | Real-world Java (50 CodeQL alerts): up to 93.3% FP recall, best F1 83.3% | p. 13 | V | weak |
345	| RQ3/RQ5 | On real-world Java, all four GPT-5 settings (incl. vanilla) filter out ≈47–67% of the true vulnerabilities (≈14–19 TPs per configuration; derived from Table 4 percentages) | p. 13 | I | weak |
346	| RQ2/RQ3 | Post-cutoff C/C++ (50 alerts): SWE-agent F1 95.5% vs vanilla 51.6%, LLM4SA-style 70.8% | p. 15 | V | weak |
347	| RQ4 | Injection CWEs filtered reliably (miss ≤2.38%); crypto/policy CWEs poorly (miss 50–84.5%) | p. 18 | V | moderate |
348	| RQ5 | Agents unsuitable for automatic suppression; human-in-the-loop needed | p. 19 | A | moderate |
349	| RQ2 | Abstract "over 92%" vs results 98.3% initial FPR; reduction reported as pp, described as % | p. 1, p. 12, p. 19 | I | weak |
350	
351	## 14. Key quotes
352	> "reducing an initial FP detection rate of over 92% on the OWASP Benchmark to as low as 6.3% in the best configuration" (p. 1)
353	> "The agent incorrectly labeled 314 true vulnerabilities as FPs, resulting in a TP retention of 77.7% and a miss rate of 22.25%." (p. 18)
354	> "LLM-based agents are unsuitable for unconditional, automatic suppression of SAST warnings" (p. 19)
355	
356	## Analyst notes
357	- Reading coverage: whole paper read (pp. 1–21 text; pp. 21–24 references only). Heatmaps (Fig. 5, Fig. 7) read from the text layer; values match the prose.
358	- Venue: peer-reviewed PACMSE (ISSTA 2026) article; the full text we hold is the arXiv v3 copy of it.
359	- Uncertainties: exact denominator for "remaining FPR" (1,325 vs 1,303) not stated; number of runs per case not stated; the Table 4 denominators (<50) are our inference from the percentages.
360

16	# To Think or Not to Think: Evaluating LLM Reasoning and Agents in Vulnerability Detection
17	
18	- Authors: Tan, Hua Beng; Widyasari, Ratnadira; Astekin, Merve; Goknil, Arda; Sözer, Hasan; Tun, Yan Naing; Husom, Erik Johannes; Shar, Lwin Khin; Jiang, Lingxiao
19	- Year / venue: 2026, Proceedings of the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (published)
20	- DOI: 10.1145/3832783.3837521 · URL: https://doi.org/10.1145/3832783.3837521
21	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` from the user-supplied publisher PDF (ACM version of record, ASE '26, 13 pages, printed pp. 2856–2868; page refs = PDF page index).
22	
23	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
24	Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.
25	
26	## 1. Research objective
27	Separate the effects of reasoning-enabled ("thinking") inference, agentic orchestration and explanation quality on LLM vulnerability detection, which prior work examined separately or under heterogeneous settings [A] (p. 1, p. 2).
28	
29	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
30	- RQ1: Do reasoning-enabled LLMs outperform non-reasoning LLMs in software vulnerability detection? [V] (p. 2)
31	- RQ2: How do multi-agent configurations compare with single-agent setups in performance, cross-setting stability and improvement consistency? [V] (p. 2)
32	- RQ3: How does explanation quality differ between thinking and non-thinking LLMs? [V] (p. 2)
33	- No formal hypotheses.
34	
35	## 3. Methodology
36	- Research design: controlled, factor-separated (factorial) experiment. RQ1: 4 models × 2 modes × 2 prompting strategies, non-agent = 16 configurations; RQ2: same × 3 agent designs = 48 configurations; RQ3 on the generated outputs [V] (p. 3, Table 1). Additional call-matched and role-sensitivity experiments (p. 10, p. 11).
37	- Approach / model / intervention: Nemotron-Nano-8B, Nemotron-Super-49B, Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-30B-A3B, each in instruct and thinking mode [V] (p. 3, p. 4). Designs: NA (direct call, no state); SA (one agent); DA (Code Author proposes, Security Analyst reviews and decides); MA (Security Researcher, Code Author, Moderator, Review Board) [V] (p. 4). Zero-shot and few-shot prompts with identical structure and examples across models/modes [V] (p. 4).
38	- Baselines or comparison conditions: instruct mode vs thinking mode; SA as the agentic baseline; call-matched self-revision with 2 and 4 calls, best-of-4 at T = 0.7, and VulAgent-lite (a specialist hypothesis–validation workflow without Joern CFG/DFG) [V] (p. 10, p. 11). No SAST tools, no fine-tuned deep-learning detectors, no proprietary LLMs as detectors.
39	
40	## 4. Dataset and sample
41	- Data source(s): PrimeVul Pair; each vulnerable function paired with a benign counterpart sharing ≥80% of its string content; the counterpart is not shown at inference [V] (p. 3, p. 5).
42	- Sample size (N) and unit: 870 functions (435 vulnerable, 435 benign) per configuration [V] (p. 3); call-matched experiments on a pair-preserving 193-pair subset, 2 largest models, zero-shot [V] (p. 11). RQ3: 120 explanations (60 snippets × 2 modes, 15 per TP/TN/FP/FN) rated by 2 blinded humans; paired tests on 59 pairs; LLM judge on a 480-explanation frame (2 models × 2 modes × 4 strata × 30) [V] (p. 5, p. 9).
43	- Sampling / selection method: full PrimeVul Pair set for RQ1/RQ2; how the 193-pair subset was chosen is not reported beyond "pair-preserving" (p. 11). No power analysis.
44	- Data availability (public? link?): replication package with code, prompts and dataset on Zenodo, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21401826 [V] (p. 5, p. 12).
45	
46	## 5. Experimental setup
47	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: vLLM v0.17–v0.18, 64K context window, NVIDIA H100 80GB on RunPod; temperature 0; pilot repetitions showed no variation, so one run per configuration [V] (p. 4). Agents built with the AG2 framework [V] (p. 4). Outputs auto-parsed to binary labels; non-conforming outputs "handled conservatively" (exact rule not reported) [V] (p. 5). LLM judge: Claude Sonnet 4.6 with 24 few-shot exemplars from held-out human ratings, validated by 5-fold cross-validation against the inter-human agreement level; Claude Opus 4.8 tried as an alternative [V] (p. 5, p. 9). Cost assumes RunPod H100 SXM at $2.69/GPU-hour [V] (p. 10).
48	- Code availability: yes, Zenodo package (p. 12).
49	
50	## 6. Evaluation metrics
51	- Metric — what it measures — why chosen: accuracy, precision, recall, F1 (directly interpretable because the data are balanced); P-C, the share of pairs where both functions are classified correctly, to measure discrimination between near-identical code (following Ding et al.) [V] (p. 5). Alert burden: false-positive rate and predicted-positive rate [V] (p. 7). Stability: mean F1, SD and coefficient of variation across settings; improvement consistency = share of matched settings beating SA [V] (p. 5). Explanations: completeness, informativeness, clarity, actionability on 1–5 Likert scales [V] (p. 5). Cost: GPU-hours, kWh, input/output tokens, USD [V] (p. 10).
52	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): Wilcoxon signed-rank with Cohen's d for RQ1/RQ2 [V] (p. 6, p. 7); Wilcoxon signed-rank with Bonferroni for paired explanation scores, Mann–Whitney for correct vs incorrect, Spearman and partial Spearman for length effects [V] (p. 5, p. 8, p. 9). No confidence intervals reported; the reasoning × orchestration interaction is not significance-tested [A] (p. 8).
53	
54	## 7. Key findings
55	1. Non-agent: thinking beats instruct F1 in 7 of 8 model–prompt settings; mean F1 0.31 → 0.41 (Wilcoxon p = 0.023, Cohen's d = 1.37); accuracy barely changes (0.518 vs 0.523, p = 0.46), so the gain is a recall shift — [V] (p. 6).
56	2. Best non-agent F1: Nemotron-Super-49B thinking zero-shot F1 0.620 (recall 0.749, precision 0.529); best non-agent P-C: Qwen3-30B-A3B instruct zero-shot 22.5% — [V] (p. 6, Table 2). Nemotron-Nano-8B stays weak (zero-shot recall 0.005–0.048) — [V] (p. 6).
57	3. Thinking improves P-C in 6 of 8 non-agent settings — [V] (p. 6).
58	4. Agent designs (means over 16 settings): SA F1 0.368 / recall 0.326 / P-C 13.7; DA F1 0.634 / recall 0.885 / precision 0.502 / P-C 6.2; MA F1 0.497 / recall 0.559 / P-C 15.8 — [V] (p. 7, Table 3).
59	5. DA flags 88.2% of functions (PPR 0.882, FPR 0.880) vs SA 30.3% (FPR 0.280) and MA 55.4% (FPR 0.549); DA vs SA F1 p < 0.0001, d = 1.40; MA vs SA p = 0.0013, d = 0.92 — [V] (p. 7).
60	6. DA beats SA on F1 in all 16 settings and is the most stable (CV 9% vs MA 32%, SA 46%); MA has the best P-C in 11 of 16 settings, DA in none — [V] (p. 7, p. 8).
61	7. Thinking's F1 benefit reverses with orchestration: ΔF1 +0.104 (NA), +0.100 (SA), −0.054 (DA), −0.066 (MA); ΔP-C stays positive (+1.9, +1.5, +8.1, +5.4) — [V] (p. 8, Table 5).
62	8. Call-matched (193 pairs, zero-shot, 2 models): 4-call self-revision has the highest mean P-C (24.7) vs SA and MA (21.9) and DA (4.7), with FPR 0.47 vs DA 0.93; the authors conclude much of the multi-agent benefit is extra inference budget — [V]/[A] (p. 11, Table 9).
63	9. Cost: thinking uses 2.7–4.4× more energy and 2.5–3.6× more output tokens; MA-thinking averages 25,533 tokens per sample vs 3,703 for NA; per configuration SA $27.5 / 8.0 h, DA $37.1 / 11.5 h, MA $52.7 / 14.4 h; all 64 configurations cost about $2,448, 481 kWh and 423.0M tokens — [V] (p. 10, Table 8).
64	10. Explanations (Nemotron-Super-49B, 59 pairs): the LLM judge rates thinking higher on completeness (+0.49), clarity (+0.51) and informativeness (+0.64); humans corroborate only informativeness (+0.30, p = 0.006) — [V] (p. 8).
65	11. Thinking explanations are 4.6× longer (13,579 vs 2,935 chars); controlling for length shrinks the judge's mode effect by about 40–60% but does not remove it; for Qwen3-30B no thinking advantage — [V] (p. 9, p. 10).
66	12. Blinded explanation quality does not differ between correct and incorrect predictions (e.g. completeness 3.58 vs 3.61, all Mann–Whitney p > 0.3); an unblinded judge creates a spurious gap (3.51 vs 2.22) — [V] (p. 9, p. 10).
67	
68	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
69	- [A] Deterministic decoding (T = 0) and a single run per configuration: results limited to deterministic decoding, no repeated-run variability (p. 11).
70	- [A] Prompt sensitivity and agent-design choices; configurations are representative, not task-optimal (p. 11).
71	- [A] Metrics may not fully capture the constructs; the rubric measures developer-facing quality, not faithfulness; a single external Claude judge may have stylistic and length preferences (p. 11).
72	- [A] Function-level PrimeVul Pair only; no project context, interprocedural reasoning or repository-level vulnerabilities; only four open Nemotron/Qwen models, larger models (DeepSeek-V3.1, Kimi-K2) not run due to hardware budget (p. 3, p. 11).
73	- [A] RQ3 manual evaluation uses a sample, which adds sampling uncertainty (p. 11).
74	- [A] The call-matched results are single runs and reported descriptively (p. 11).
75	
76	## 9. Limitations we identified
77	- [I] An "always vulnerable" classifier scores F1 = 0.667 on this balanced set (precision 0.5, recall 1.0). No reported configuration exceeds it (Table 3 max 0.665, Table 9 max 0.666), so DA's "highest F1" is near the trivial flag-everything point. Based on Table 3 (p. 7) and Table 9 (p. 11).
78	- [I] All P-C values are ≤26.9%, i.e. at or below the 25% that a random guesser labelling each pair member independently can reach at most (q(1−q) ≤ 0.25 for flag rate q); only self-revision slightly exceeds it (25.9–26.9%, Table 9). DA is far below that ceiling: 0.7–18.8% per setting, mean 6.2% (Table 3, p. 7), and 0.5–13.0% in Table 9 (p. 11). Absolute discrimination is therefore weak in every design. Based on Tables 2, 3, 4 and 9 (p. 6, p. 7, p. 11).
79	- [I] No SAST or deep-learning baselines, so the paper says nothing about LLMs vs traditional tools. Based on Table 1 (p. 3).
80	- [I] Training-data contamination is not discussed; PrimeVul is public and the open models may have seen it. Based on a search of the full text for contamination or memorisation (none found).
81	- [I] Statistical tests on 8 or 16 paired configuration-level means have little power and no correction across RQ1/RQ2 tests; differences between individual cells should not be over-read (the authors say this too, p. 6).
82	- [I] Wording conflict: the abstract and conclusion say explanation gains are "largely" length-mediated (p. 11), while Section 4.3 says "substantially but not wholly" (40–60%) (p. 9).
83	- [I] Selection of the 193-pair subset and the handling of non-conforming outputs are not described, which limits checks on Table 9. Based on p. 5, p. 11.
84	
85	## 10. Threats to validity
86	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): agent designs differ in number of calls and context, partly controlled by call-matched baselines (p. 7, p. 11); possible pretraining contamination not addressed; parsing rule for non-conforming outputs unspecified (p. 5).
87	- External (generalisability of sample/context): function-level C/C++, one benchmark, four mid-size open models (p. 11).
88	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): F1 on balanced data rewards over-flagging (authors pair it with P-C, p. 7); explanation rubric measures perceived quality, not faithfulness (p. 11).
89	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): single runs; small numbers of paired configuration means; Bonferroni applied only in RQ3 (p. 8, p. 9).
90	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): good — open models, vLLM versions, hardware, prompts and replication package on Zenodo (p. 4, p. 12).
91	
92	## 11. Future research directions
93	- Stated by authors [A]: more reasoning-oriented families (distilled DeepSeek-R1, Gemma) and larger models; costlier repository-level settings with dependency resolution, retrieval and tool support (p. 11); deeper per-model analysis and significance testing of the reasoning × orchestration interaction (p. 8).
94	- Suggested by us [I]: report the trivial flag-all and random baselines alongside F1/P-C; add SAST and fine-tuned DL baselines on the same pairs; repeat runs with non-zero temperature for variance.
95	
96	## 12. Relevance to our research
97	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1 (LLM-only variants), RQ2, RQ3, RQ5.
98	- How it informs our work [I]: controlled evidence that reasoning modes and multi-agent designs mainly shift the recall/false-positive trade-off rather than improving discrimination, with detailed energy, token and USD costs. Useful for RQ3 (cost vs benefit of agentic LLM designs) and RQ2 (F1 vs pairwise metrics), and consistent with yildiz2025benchmarking's finding that F1 hides near-random pairwise accuracy. No traditional or DL baseline, so it does not inform LLM-vs-SAST directly.
99

104	| RQ1 | Best function-level F1 on PrimeVul Pair is 0.620 (Nemotron-Super-49B thinking) and best non-agent P-C 22.5%, i.e. weak discrimination of vulnerable vs patched functions | p. 6 | V | moderate |

141	# Benchmarking LLMs and LLM-based Agents in Practical Vulnerability Detection for Code Repositories
142	
143	- Authors: Yildiz, Alperen; Teo, Sin G; Lou, Yiling; Feng, Yebo; Wang, Chong; Divakaran, Dinil Mon
144	- Year / venue: 2025, Proceedings of the 63rd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers) (published)
145	- DOI: 10.18653/v1/2025.acl-long.1490 · URL: https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2025.acl-long.1490
146	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index; printed pages 30848–30865). Identity confirmed: title and authors on p. 1 match metadata.
147	
148	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
149	Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.
150	
151	## 1. Research objective
152	Provide a practical benchmark for just-in-time (JIT, i.e. commit-triggered) repository-level vulnerability detection with interprocedural context and pairwise (vulnerable vs patched) evaluation, and use it to compare LLMs with LLM-based ReAct agents [A] (p. 1, p. 2).
153	
154	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
155	- No numbered RQs. Four comparisons: detection method (p. 7), prompting strategy (p. 8), foundation model (p. 8), pairwise error analysis (p. 8) [V].
156	- Three stated requirements for practical benchmarks: interprocedural context, scalability, pairwise comparison [V] (p. 3, p. 4).
157	
158	## 3. Methodology
159	- Research design: benchmark construction plus comparative evaluation [V] (p. 4, p. 5).
160	- Approach / model / intervention: (1) Plain LLM — target function only; (2) Dep-Aug LLM — adds Top-5 lexically similar callers/callees (Jaccard), reproducing VulEval; (3) ReAct agent with tools get_callers, get_callees, get_definition (CFlow + CTags, LangChain) [V] (p. 5, p. 6). Each in four variants: vanilla, CoT ("Solve this problem step by step..."), few-shot (10 hand-made vulnerable/benign pairs from CWE Top-25 web pages), CoT+FS [V] (p. 5, p. 6).
161	- Baselines or comparison conditions: the three LLM settings against each other; no SAST tools, no fine-tuned deep-learning detectors [V] (p. 5). A random-guessing reference (22.70%) is cited from Ding et al. (p. 7).
162	
163	## 4. Dataset and sample
164	- Data source(s): PrimeVul (CVE fixed in a single commit modifying a single function); vul-intro commit approximated by tracing the target function's history back to its last modification into the vulnerable version [V] (p. 4, p. 5).
165	- Sample size (N) and unit: 879 CVEs, 91 CWEs (max 10 CVEs per CWE), 1,758 samples (879 vul, 879 ben) [V] (p. 4, p. 5). Repositories: mean 2,955.9 files, 91% C / 9% C++, mean 988.8 KLoC (median 297.6, SD 1,991.2); target function mean 696.4 LOC [V] (p. 5).
166	- Sampling / selection method: random selection of 879 PrimeVul CVEs ensuring CWE coverage [V] (p. 4).
167	- Data availability (public? link?): "We release all code and data at this repository" (p. 2); the URL is a hyperlink not present in the extracted text.
168	
169	## 5. Experimental setup
170	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: GPT-4o-mini and GPT-4o at temperature 0; Transformers v4.52.0, LangChain v0.3.14 [V] (p. 6). Llama-3.1-8B and DeepSeek-Coder-V2-16B in Appendix B [V] (p. 8, p. 15). Number of runs: not reported (one implied by temperature 0). Number of pairs evaluated per setting: not reported (see Analyst notes). Token use, cost and runtime: not reported.
171	- Code availability: yes, per p. 2.
172	
173	## 6. Evaluation metrics
174	- Metric — what it measures — why chosen: F1 (common metric) and pairwise accuracy pAcc = share of pairs where both versions are labelled correctly, inspired by PrimeVul, to test whether methods capture the vulnerability rather than surface patterns [V] (p. 6). Error types: pairwise vulnerable, pairwise benign, pairwise reversed [V] (p. 8).
175	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): none reported.
176	
177	## 7. Key findings
178	1. GPT-4o-mini F1/pAcc — Plain: 56.00/3.36 (vanilla), 65.10/3.36 (CoT), 48.74/7.56 (FS), 64.65/11.76 (CoT+FS); Dep-Aug: 52.68/2.05, 66.05/4.86, 48.23/7.27, 65.01/4.68; ReAct: 56.63/12.61, 56.93/16.81, 56.81/20.17, 51.06/14.29 — [V] (p. 6, Table 2).
179	2. GPT-4o F1/pAcc — Plain: 65.96/1.02, 62.22/15.02, 62.77/4.44, 64.44/17.63; Dep-Aug: 63.30/1.03, 62.60/18.66, 62.03/2.39, 61.12/18.79; ReAct: 57.77/17.63, 58.07/19.13, 56.42/18.91, 52.61/18.89 — [V] (p. 6, Table 2).
180	3. ReAct agents have higher pAcc than other methods for every prompting strategy (gains 0.1 to 16.61 points); Plain/Dep-Aug have higher F1 in most settings (4.15–13.95 points) — [V] (p. 7). Average ReAct pAcc gain over Dep-Aug: 9.46 (4o-mini) and 8.42 (4o) — [V] (p. 7).
181	4. LLM methods label >90% of samples vulnerable in some settings; precision is around 50% for all methods on the balanced benchmark, so F1 rewards over-prediction — [V]/[A] (p. 7).
182	5. On the original non-paired PrimeVul test set (695 vul / 25,216 ben), GPT-4o-mini F1 falls to 5.41–12.21 — [V] (p. 7, Table 3).
183	6. Dep-Aug does not consistently beat Plain and sometimes lowers pAcc, possibly due to noisy retrieved context — [V]/[A] (p. 7).
184	7. The most common pairwise error is "both vulnerable": ~40–95% for LLMs, ~35–50% for ReAct — [V] (p. 8).
185	8. ReAct calls tools far more on the vulnerable than the benign version (5.85 vs 1.79, GPT-4o-mini vanilla) — inconsistent analysis — [V] (p. 9).
186	9. Llama-3.1-8B ReAct agents often fail output formatting and default to "benign" (F1 3.28–14.67); DeepSeek-Coder-V2 Dep-Aug with CoT+FS reaches F1 82.09 and pAcc 69.24, the best result in the paper, while its ReAct agent stays at pAcc ≤21.39 — [V] (p. 8, p. 15, Table 4).
187	
188	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
189	- [A] Vul-intro commits may be traced imperfectly; some instances manually inspected (p. 9).
190	- [A] Label-balanced dataset may bias F1 comparisons (p. 9).
191	- [A] Missing statistics such as the share of interprocedural vulnerabilities; annotation hard to scale (p. 9).
192	
193	## 9. Limitations we identified
194	- [I] No SAST or deep-learning baselines and no cost data, so the paper cannot answer LLM-vs-SAST/DL questions directly. Based on p. 5–6.
195	- [I] All GPT-4o/4o-mini settings have pAcc ≤20.17%, below the 25% expected from independent random labelling of each pair member; "ReAct is better" means "less bad". Based on Table 2 (p. 6).
196	- [I] The headline "ReAct agents better at pairwise" is not robust across models: with DeepSeek-Coder-V2, Dep-Aug LLM is far better (pAcc 69.24 vs ≤21.39). Based on Table 4 (p. 15).
197	- [I] Data leakage is not discussed: PrimeVul CVEs and fixes are public and likely in GPT-4o training data. Based on p. 4 (no contamination analysis found in the text).
198	- [I] No repeated runs, variance or significance tests; differences of a few points (e.g. 0.1-point pAcc gain) are not interpretable. Based on p. 6–7.
199	- [I] Few-shot examples are single-function CWE web-page snippets, which may not suit interprocedural agents (authors note this too, p. 8).
200	
201	## 10. Threats to validity
202	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): possible pretraining contamination; vul-intro approximation (p. 9); unclear per-setting sample sizes.
203	- External (generalisability of sample/context): C/C++ only (91% C), PrimeVul single-function fixes, OpenAI models mainly (p. 5, p. 6).
204	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): pAcc captures discrimination of vulnerable vs patched code; F1 on a balanced set overstates usefulness (p. 7).
205	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): no tests, no variance, many configurations compared.
206	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): code and data released (p. 2); prompts in Appendix A (p. 12, p. 13).
207	
208	## 11. Future research directions
209	- Stated by authors [A]: evaluation guidelines for JIT benchmarking; agent-oriented prompting strategies; robust reasoning models for vulnerability analysis (p. 2, p. 8); more benign commits for F1 (p. 9); code-specific LLMs optimised for agents (p. 15); integrate constraint solving or program analysis (p. 9).
210	- Suggested by us [I]: add SAST (CodeQL/Semgrep) and fine-tuned DL baselines on JITVul pairs; report cost and contamination checks.
211	
212	## 12. Relevance to our research
213	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1 (LLM-only), RQ2, RQ5.
214	- How it informs our work [I]: mainly methodological evidence for RQ2 — F1 on balanced data looks moderate (~50–66%) while pairwise accuracy shows near-random discrimination, explaining why reported LLM effectiveness varies across studies. No direct LLM-vs-SAST comparison.
215	
216	## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
217	| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
218	|---|---|---|---|---|
219	| RQ1 | GPT-4o/4o-mini plain, dependency-augmented and ReAct detectors reach F1 48–66% but pairwise accuracy only 1.02–20.17% on 879 CVE pairs | p. 6 | V | moderate |
220	| RQ1 | ReAct agents give the highest pAcc for every prompting strategy with GPT-4o/4o-mini (gains up to 16.61 points) | p. 7 | V | weak |
221	| RQ2 | F1 is distribution-sensitive: GPT-4o-mini F1 drops from ~49–65% (balanced pairs) to 5.41–12.21% on non-paired PrimeVul (695 vul / 25,216 ben) | p. 6, p. 7 | V | moderate |
222	| RQ2 | LLM methods label >90% of samples vulnerable in some settings, with precision ~50%, inflating F1 | p. 7 | V | moderate |
223	| RQ2 | With DeepSeek-Coder-V2, Dep-Aug LLM reaches F1 82.09 / pAcc 69.24, contradicting the agent advantage seen with GPT models | p. 15 | V | weak |
224	| RQ5 | Most frequent failure is labelling both vulnerable and patched versions vulnerable (40–95% of LLM failures); agents analyse pairs inconsistently | p. 8, p. 9 | V | moderate |
225	
226	## 14. Key quotes
227	> "A higher F1 score does not necessarily indicate a detection method's superior ability to capture vulnerability characteristics." (p. 7)
228	
229	> "precision remains similar across methods, around 50%, as observed on our label-balanced benchmark" (p. 7)
230	
231	## Analyst notes
232	- Reading coverage: all 18 PDF pages read, including Appendices A–C (prompts, Llama/DeepSeek results, case studies CVE-2019-15164 and CVE-2019-3877).
233	- Uncertainties: the number of pairs per setting is not stated. Every Plain and ReAct pAcc for GPT-4o-mini and Llama-3.1 is an exact multiple of 1/119 (e.g. 3.36 = 4/119, 20.17 = 24/119, 0.84 = 1/119), while GPT-4o values match k/879. This suggests some settings were evaluated on ~119 pairs, or after excluding failed runs, but the paper does not say so; treat cross-setting comparisons cautiously ([I], arithmetic on Table 2 p. 6 and Table 4 p. 15). "Improvements ... 0.1% to 16.61%" are percentage points. The 22.70% random-guessing figure is cited from Ding et al., not computed here (p. 7). Quote 2 is joined across a hyphenated line break ("sim-ilar").

## G1: Published results are not re-scored against trivial baselines or realistic prevalence; no shared evaluation protocol exists for comparing LLMs, SAST and DL
- Gap type: methodological
- Evidence that the gap exists:
  - **Results sit at the flag-everything level.** On 50/50 data, "flag everything" gives F1 0.667. Studies with balanced data report best values at or below that level:
    - shu: the dummy classifier scores 0.6693 against a best of 0.7075 [@shu2026evaluating, p. 11; @shu2026evaluating, p. 17] [V];
    - tan: best F1 0.665–0.666 [@tan2026think, p. 7];
    - yildiz: GPT F1 48–66 [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 6];
    - khare: always-vulnerable rows appear among the best F1 values [@khare2025understanding, p. 16].
  - **The same pattern holds at other prevalences, in three more recent studies** (second pass). Two of them report trivial baselines themselves; for the third the chance level is derivable:
    - deininger (35.4% vulnerable sample): LLM F1 0.405–0.615 against always-vulnerable F1 0.523 [@deininger2026open, p. 7] [V]. At the natural 1:44 prevalence every LLM's precision is 2.3–3.8% against 2.21% for always-flag, with 25.6–41.9 false positives per true positive [@deininger2026open, p. 8] [V] (2.8–4.6% in the budget-matched second epoch [@deininger2026open, p. 17]).
    - tashenova (PHP): a one-feature token-count baseline matches or beats the TF-IDF random forest in 4 of 6 settings and is within 0.001 macro-F1 of the Bi-LSTM [@tashenova2026real, p. 8] [V]. The authors ask that future detectors "be required to clear such trivial baselines" [@tashenova2026real, p. 13] [A].
    - lu (VentiVul, post-May-2025 CVEs, prevalence 263/13,326 = 1.97% [@lu2025lab, p. 4]): DL F1 is 3.47–8.65 [@lu2025lab, p. 13] [V]. The paper reports no trivial baseline; by our calculation the all-positive F1 is 3.87%, and 7 of the 12 LLM conservative F1 values fall below it [@lu2025lab, p. 14] [I].
  - **Class balance flips rankings.**
    - shu: fine-tuned GPT-4o wins on balanced data, but PLMs win on the 17%-vulnerable test [@shu2026evaluating, p. 17; @shu2026evaluating, p. 40] [V].
    - yildiz: F1 falls from about 49–65 to 5.41–12.21 on non-paired data [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 7] [V].
  - **Scoring is unequal between families.**
    - gnieciak applies a lenient location rule only to LLMs [@gnieciak2025large, p. 6] [V].
    - The CASTLE prompt reveals the scoring scheme to the LLM [@dubniczky2025castle, p. 9] [V].
    - Statement-level scoring halves F1 [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 8] [V].
  - **Headline LLM-vs-SAST numbers use five incompatible metrics**: macro F1, CASTLE score, accuracy, detection ratio, recall/SFDR [@gnieciak2025large, p. 10; @dubniczky2025castle, p. 10; @khare2025understanding, p. 9; @zhou2024comparison, p. 5; @li2026llm, p. 11] [I].
  - **Spurious baselines and random references:**
    - a word-count classifier reaches F1 0.86 on BigVul [@risse2025top, p. 11] [V];
    - GPT-4 pairwise correctness is below the 22.70% random reference [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9] [V].
  - **Statistics are rare.** Among the first 16 primary studies, only tan2026think applies significance tests to its main comparison [@tan2026think, p. 6] [I, our count]. Of the four second-pass papers, deininger2026open uses a paired bootstrap with Holm correction [@deininger2026open, p. 6] [V].
  - **The decision rule and the prompt can flip conclusions.** At the default argmax threshold the fine-tuned PrimeVul detector predicts all-safe despite ROC-AUC 0.845; the authors nearly reported this as "trained detectors are no better than LLMs" [@deininger2026open, p. 11] [V]. Prompt paraphrases change the winning LLM [@deininger2026open, p. 20] [V].
  - **Authors call for guidelines.** yildiz2025benchmarking calls for evaluation guidelines for JIT benchmarking [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 2] [A]. ding2025vulnerability proposes VD-S because accuracy and F1 mislead [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 2] [A]. lu2025lab asks for cross-dataset and temporally separated testing plus patch-pair metrics [@lu2025lab, p. 16] [A].
- Novelty check (2026-11-12; first pass Q4, Q5, Q9, Q10 on OpenAlex/arXiv from 2024/2025 and W4; second pass Q35 on OpenAlex/Crossref from 2025). Closest work:
  - **In our corpus, within-study baselines only.** shu2026evaluating, deininger2026open and tashenova2026real report trivial baselines, and lu2025lab's chance level is derivable (see evidence above). PrimeVul's VD-S is also in the corpus. Each applies the baseline only to its own results; none re-scores other studies [I].
  - **qin2026review** (in corpus) recommends better reporting [@qin2026review, p. 13] but recomputes no published results; its only quantitative re-report repeats ding2025vulnerability's table [@qin2026review, p. 12; @ding2025vulnerability, p. 7] [I].
  - *Pitfalls in Machine Learning for Computer Security* (CACM 2024, doi:10.1145/3643456) and *Pitfalls in LMs for Code Intelligence* (TOSEM 2025, doi:10.1145/3748647): generic pitfall catalogues with no re-scoring of vulnerability-detection results.
  - *How much model does warning triage need?* (American Impact Review 2026, doi:10.66308/air.e80134906): re-scores models against a simple reference with MCC and bootstrap CIs, but for actionable-warning triage, not vulnerability detection, and in an unknown-tier venue.
  - *On-premise open-weight LLMs for interpretable web vulnerability detection* (TSARKA Science 2026, doi:10.66571/tsarka-3134-6057-11; abstract only, from Q32): notes that several configurations "approach the score of a classifier labelling every input as vulnerable" and proposes reporting specificity. Again within one study (120 snippets).
  - Q35 returned no relevant hit.

  We found no study that recomputes published LLM, SAST and DL vulnerability-detection results *across studies* against trivial baselines and realistic prevalence (searches on 2026-11-12).
- **Second-pass verdict: unchanged (still open).** Trivial baselines are spreading as a *within-study* practice. This makes the gap's premise stronger: four further studies (deininger, tashenova, lu, and the abstract-only TSARKA study) show results at or near trivial levels. It does not fill the gap, because none of them re-scores other studies' published numbers on a common scale [I]. The contribution should now be framed as a *systematic cross-study* re-scoring, and it must credit these within-study baselines rather than claim to be the first to use them.
- Confidence: **medium–high**. The evidence now comes from ≥9 independent primary studies. The only risk is an unpublished or non-indexed meta-analysis.
- Potential contribution: a "re-scored results table" that makes the review's central claim concrete. Many reported LLM advantages may vanish or reverse once compared with flag-all baselines and evaluated at realistic prevalence. It also yields a minimal reporting checklist (confusion matrix, prevalence, trivial baselines, unit and location rule, runs/variance).
- Suggested study (secondary analysis of published numbers; no model runs):
  - **Data:** results tables of the 20 primary studies (plus any added papers). Extract every (study, tool, dataset, configuration) row that reports enough to rebuild a confusion matrix: TP/FP/FN/TN, or P, R and prevalence.
  - **Sample:** all extractable rows. Rows without prevalence or FPR are listed separately, not dropped silently.
  - **Method:** for each row compute:
    - MCC;
    - Youden's J = recall − FPR;
    - ΔF1 = F1 − F1_flag-all, where F1_flag-all = 2π/(1+π) and π is prevalence;
    - precision at deployment prevalence (π = 1%, 5%, 17%) via P = R·π / (R·π + FPR·(1−π)).
  - **Baselines:** always-vulnerable; random (P-C reference 22.70% for ding-style pairs); published dummy, word-count or token-count baselines where available. Use a study's own published baseline where it exists (shu, deininger, tashenova) and check that our formula reproduces it; this is a built-in validity check of the re-scoring.
  - **Analysis:** within each study, rank tools before and after re-scoring and count rank reversals (Kendall τ). Do not pool across datasets marked "not comparable" in methodology comparison §3. Report how many rows fail to beat flag-all.
  - **Threats:** many rows lack TN/FPR (selection bias); rounding in published tables; lenient TP definitions cannot be undone after the fact; transcription errors (mitigate by double extraction and spot-checking against PDFs).
- Feasibility for a beginner: **easy**. Needs only a spreadsheet or about 50 lines of Python, no GPU and no API cost, and takes about 2–4 weeks. It can be included directly in the comparative review as an added-value table.

## G2: No same-benchmark, leakage-controlled comparison of LLMs vs semantic SAST vs fine-tuned DL on real, post-cutoff code with file or repository context
- Gap type: evidence / methodological
- **Second-pass verdict: narrowed.** deininger2026open fills the function-level, pre-cutoff, C/C++ version of this gap with lightweight SAST. What remains open: (a) post-cutoff targets, (b) file or repository context, (c) a semantic, build-based SAST arm such as CodeQL, and (d) a peer-reviewed non-C/C++ version (a function-level Python/Java/JS three-family preprint exists, abstract only; see novelty check).
- Evidence that the gap exists:
  - **Two studies in our corpus run all three families; each covers only part of the needed setting.**
    - khare2025understanding evaluates LLMs, SAST and DL, but CodeQL runs on synthetic data only [@khare2025understanding, p. 7] [V].
    - deininger2026open runs 8 zero-shot LLMs, Flawfinder 2.0.20, Cppcheck 2.21, Semgrep 1.175 and two CodeBERT detectors on the same 1549 PrimeVul C/C++ functions [@deininger2026open, p. 6; @deininger2026open, p. 10] [V]. Its limits are the ones that define what is left of G2:
      - CodeQL could not be run because the functions are unbuildable snippets [@deininger2026open, p. 10] [V];
      - all CVEs date from 2008–2022 and predate the models' training cutoffs, and recall is 7–15 points higher on pre-2020 CVEs [@deininger2026open, p. 24] [V];
      - function level, one dataset, C/C++ only [@deininger2026open, p. 25] [A];
      - the fine-tuned detector is in-distribution while the LLMs are zero-shot [@deininger2026open, p. 11] [A].
    - Its result shows why the gap still matters: the ranking depends on the metric. On balanced accuracy fine-tuned CodeBERT leads (0.765 vs ≤0.711 for LLMs); on precision at 1:44 prevalence Semgrep (26.0%, CI 5.7–66.9%) and strict Flawfinder (13.4%) lead, and every LLM is at 2.3–3.8% in the first epoch (2.8–4.6% budget-matched) [@deininger2026open, p. 8; @deininger2026open, p. 10; @deininger2026open, p. 17] [V].
  - **zhou2024comparison has no classic DL detector.** It compares fine-tuned and prompted LLMs with SAST [@zhou2024comparison, p. 4] [V].
  - **Temporal out-of-distribution evidence exists, but without SAST.** lu2025lab tests DL and four open LLMs on VentiVul, built from Linux and Chromium CVEs disclosed from 1 May 2025 [@lu2025lab, p. 4] [V]. LineVul falls from F1 91–94.5 in distribution [@lu2025lab, p. 12] to 4.39–6.87 on VentiVul, and all 8 DL configurations score 3.47–8.65 [@lu2025lab, p. 13] [V]. No static-analysis tool is evaluated [I]. The authors cannot fully exclude LLM contamination because pre-training cutoffs are unknown [@lu2025lab, p. 17] [A].
  - **PHP evidence exists, but without LLMs or a standard SAST tool.** tashenova2026real compares an in-house taint analyser with ML and LSTM detectors under plugin-grouped, de-duplicated folds [@tashenova2026real, p. 5] [V]; no LLM or transformer was run [@tashenova2026real, p. 13] [V].
  - **Studies that call for this comparison:**
    - chakraborty2024revisiting: evaluate static and dynamic analysis tools on Real-Vul [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 13] [A];
    - ding2025vulnerability: hybrid LM + program-analysis systems [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 10] [A].
  - **Results reverse across setups.**
    - LLM vs SAST rankings reverse between small programs, synthetic suites and repositories [@gnieciak2025large, p. 10; @khare2025understanding, p. 9; @li2026llm, p. 7] [V].
    - LLM vs DL rankings reverse with dataset and class balance [@fu2023chatgpt, p. 4; @ding2025vulnerability, p. 9; @shu2026evaluating, p. 40] [V].
  - **Contamination and leakage are rarely controlled.**
    - Exact-copy leakage reaches up to 18.9% [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 4] [V].
    - Benchmarks are probably in pre-training data [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 30] [A], and post-cutoff datasets are recommended [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 38] [A].
    - Only xiong2026sifting, li2026llm and lu2025lab test on post-cutoff or temporally separated code [@xiong2026sifting, p. 15; @li2026llm, p. 5; @lu2025lab, p. 4] [V]; none of the three runs all three families [I].
  - **Survey future work asks only for verified benchmarks.** The surveys' future directions call for verified, contamination-free, repository-level benchmarks [@zhou2025large, p. 22; @sheng2025llms, p. 25] [A], but not for a controlled three-family comparison [I]. deininger2026open plans a post-cutoff restriction [@deininger2026open, p. 24] [A].
- Novelty check (2026-11-12; first pass Q6, Q7, Q8 on OpenAlex/arXiv/Crossref from 2024/2025, contamination angle Q19, Q20, W3, W6; second pass Q27, Q28, Q29 on OpenAlex/Crossref from 2025, arXiv abstract page A2, W10).
  - **Now in our corpus (analysed):** deininger2026open (three families, function level, pre-cutoff, lightweight SAST), lu2025lab (post-cutoff, no SAST), tashenova2026real (PHP, no LLM). See evidence above.
  - **Dahiya et al. 2026**, *Are Frontier LLMs Ready for Cybersecurity? Evidence for Vertical Foundation Models from Dual-Mode Vulnerability Benchmarks* (arXiv 2605.23243, preprint, v5 June 2026; **abstract only**, A2). Six frontier and two domain-specialised models on (i) white-box *function-level* detection in C/Java/Python built on VulnLLM-R and (ii) black-box testing of five web applications with 118 known vulnerabilities. From the abstract: no SAST baseline (the only tools named are Playwright and Burp Suite MCP servers for black-box testing), no fine-tuned DL detector, no post-cutoff or leakage control mentioned. Its "application-level" track is black-box dynamic testing, not source-code analysis. **Does not fill G2.**

content.content:
## G3: True-positive loss in LLM filtering of SAST alarms is not controlled per CWE on real security alerts
- Gap type: practical / methodological
- Evidence that the gap exists:
  - **xiong2026sifting.** The best agent configuration cuts OWASP FPR from 98.3% to 6.3% [@xiong2026sifting, p. 12] but drops 22.25% of true vulnerabilities [@xiong2026sifting, p. 18] [V].
    - The miss rate is low for injection CWEs (CWE-78 2.38%, CWE-89 1.10%, CWE-79 0.41%) [V].
    - It is 77.17% for weak cryptography and 84.50% for weak hashing [@xiong2026sifting, p. 18] [V].
    - The authors plan "CWE-aware, cost-adaptive agent strategies and human-in-the-loop" auditing [@xiong2026sifting, p. 20] [A].
  - **du2026reducing.** Removes 94–98% of false alarms with real-bug recall of 0.75–0.88 [@du2026reducing, p. 8] [V]. This covers non-security bug types and the authors' own method.
  - **Recommended but not evaluated.** kaniewski2026systematic recommends SAST → LLM false-positive filtering pipelines [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 42] [A] but its corpus excludes them [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 8].
  - **Real-world samples are small.** xiong uses 50 alerts per set [@xiong2026sifting, p. 13] [V].
- Novelty check (2026-11-12; Q13, Q14, Q24 on OpenAlex/arXiv/Crossref from 2024/2025, plus Q25; W5). Closest hits, all not analysed:
  - *ZeroFalse* (arXiv 2510.02534): CWE-specific context, high F1 on OWASP/OpenVuln, claims to preserve coverage.
  - *Using LLMs to Adjudicate Static-Analysis Alerts with Error Reduction Techniques* (arXiv 2607.09979): consistency checks reach ≥98% recall on Juliet, FormAI and SV-COMP, which are synthetic suites.
  - *QASecClaw* (arXiv 2605.01885): multi-agent FP reduction on OWASP.
  - *Case-Level Verification in Scanner-LLM Cascades* (arXiv 2610.08406): formalises the FP-reduction vs TPR trade-off, but for DAST.
  - *Trusting the Tool* (arXiv 2610.32876): false analyser assurances lower detection of real vulnerabilities by up to 19 points.

  These show that TP loss is being measured, and can be reduced on synthetic suites. We found no study that tests a CWE-aware selective filtering policy, i.e. one that filters only CWE classes with demonstrated low miss rates, with held-out evaluation and full FP-reduction vs TP-retention curves on real-world security alerts (searches on 2026-11-12).
- Confidence: **low–medium**. This is an active area with many 2025–26 preprints. The gap is narrow and could be filled quickly.
- **Second-pass verdict: unchanged.** None of the four new papers studies LLM filtering of SAST alarms, and the second-pass cost/triage queries (Q30, Q31) surfaced only items already listed above (arXiv 2607.09979) or non-security triage work. Not re-searched separately.
- Potential contribution: an operating-point view of alarm filtering, i.e. what share of real vulnerabilities is lost per CWE for a given FP reduction. Also a simple routing policy that practitioners can adopt.
- Suggested study:
  - **Data:**
    - OWASP Benchmark v1.2 (Java, 2,740 labelled cases, official scorer) for development.
    - A real-world set of about 100 SAST alerts from post-cutoff open-source Java projects, labelled by two raters (κ), for testing.
  - **Method:** run Semgrep and CodeQL; ask 2 open LLMs (7–8B) for a TP/FP verdict with a confidence score, 3 runs.
  - **Policies:**
    - no filter;
    - filter-all (xiong's vanilla);
    - CWE-aware filter that applies the LLM only to CWEs whose miss rate was below 5% on a development half of OWASP, evaluated on the other half and on the real set.
  - **Metrics:** FP-reduction rate; TP retention; residual FPR; expected triage cost = c_FP·FP + c_FN·FN for cost ratios 1:10 to 1:100.
  - **Analysis:** curves across confidence thresholds; per-CWE bootstrap CIs.
  - **Threats:** OWASP is synthetic and probably in pre-training data; per-CWE cells are small; rater bias.
- Feasibility for a beginner: **easy–moderate**. Ground truth and the scorer are public, Java SAST on OWASP builds easily, and 7B models run locally. Expect 4–6 weeks. The main effort is labelling the real-world alerts.

## G4: Hybrid LLM+SAST detectors lack independent replication that separates target, metric and labeller effects
- Gap type: contradiction / evidence
- Evidence that the gap exists:
  - **RepoAudit: author evaluation vs independent evaluation.**
    - Authors: 78.43% precision and all 21 known bugs reproduced, one run per setting [@guo2025repoaudit, p. 8; @guo2025repoaudit, p. 17] [V].
    - Independent (li2026llm): 0 of 110 known C/C++ vulnerabilities and 92.77% SFDR [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 11] [V]; cost up to $1,247.66 per project [@li2026llm, p. 16] [V].
  - **IRIS: author evaluation vs independent evaluation.**
    - Authors: 55 vs 27 of 120 CVEs detected compared with CodeQL [@li2024iris, p. 8] [V].
    - Independent: 97.80% vs 77.00% SFDR on new Java projects [@li2026llm, p. 12] [V].
  - **The independent study labels with an LLM it also evaluates.** li2026llm labels warnings with Codex, which it also evaluates [@li2026llm, p. 11] [V], so its labeller is not independent [I].
  - **The gain depends on a strong LLM.** IRIS gains depend on GPT-4; smaller LLMs worsen FDR [@li2024iris, p. 10] [V].
  - **Neither paper settles the discrepancy** (methodology comparison §4, C2/C6) [I].
- Novelty check (2026-11-12; Q11, Q12, Q23 on arXiv/OpenAlex/Crossref from 2024/2025; W3). Closest hits:
  - li2026llm (in corpus) is itself the only independent re-evaluation.
  - *What Survives the Next Model?* (arXiv 2609.00468): re-runs ICSE 2026 technique papers against single prompts, across SE tasks generally.
  - *Trusting the Tool* (arXiv 2610.32876): studies LLM deference to analyser evidence, not tool replication.
  - Agent tools found (Revelio arXiv 2606.22263, AnyPoC arXiv 2604.11950) are new tools, not replications.

  We found no study that re-runs IRIS or RepoAudit on the authors' original benchmark and on new targets, under the same blinded human labelling, so that the discrepancy can be attributed (searches on 2026-11-12).
- Confidence: **medium**. Reproductions may exist in artifact-evaluation reports that are not indexed.
- **Second-pass verdict: unchanged.** None of the four new papers evaluates IRIS, RepoAudit or another hybrid LLM+SAST detector. Not re-searched separately.
- Potential contribution: tells practitioners whether published hybrid gains transfer to new code. It also tells researchers which evaluation choices (targets, metric, labeller, model version) drive the reported differences.
- Suggested study:
  - **Design:** 2 × 2 factorial — target set (original CWE-Bench-Java subset vs post-cutoff Java CVEs) × metric (the original "detected CVE" metric vs sampled false-discovery rate), on the **same** runs.
  - **Data:** 30 CWE-Bench-Java CVEs across 4 CWEs, plus 10–15 post-cutoff Java CVEs. IRIS code and data are public [@li2024iris, p. 2].
  - **Arms:** IRIS with the original LLM family where affordable, and with one open model; CodeQL alone as baseline.
  - **Labelling:** a random sample of ≥100 warnings labelled by two humans blinded to the tool (κ reported).
  - **Metrics:** detections, FDR/SFDR, cost (tokens, USD, time).
  - **Threats:** model deprecation (GPT-4 versions); CodeQL version drift; build failures; API cost.
- Feasibility for a beginner: **moderate–hard**. Building Java projects for CodeQL and running a hybrid pipeline is demanding. A reduced IRIS-only replication on 20–30 CVEs with an open model is feasible in about 8 weeks. RepoAudit (C/C++, high token cost) is not recommended for a beginner.

## G5: Real-CVE LLM-vs-standard-SAST evidence is missing for PHP and Go (JavaScript and Python only partly covered)
## G5: Real-CVE LLM-vs-standard-SAST evidence is missing for PHP and Go (JavaScript and Python only partly covered)
- Gap type: population/context
- **Second-pass verdict: narrowed.** LLM-only evidence on real WordPress-plugin (PHP) vulnerabilities now exists (Neef et al. 2026, abstract only), and a function-level three-family comparison exists for Python, Java and JavaScript (arXiv 2503.01449, abstract only). What remains open is a comparison
- Evidence that the gap exists:
  - **The literature is concentrated on C/C++ and Java.**
    - Evidence is concentrated on C/C++ and Java [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 28] [V].
    - 555 mappable CWEs appear in no analysed dataset [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 34] [V].
    - Directions call for Python, Java, Rust and multilingual benchmarks [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 40] [A].
  - **Authors list other languages as future work:**
    - RepoAudit: extension to Python and JavaScript [@guo2025repoaudit, p. 10] [A];
    - IRIS: other languages [@li2024iris, p. 10] [A];
    - du2026reducing: more languages [@du2026reducing, p. 10] [A];
    - xiong2026sifting: more languages and SAST tools [@xiong2026sifting, p. 20] [A];
    - li2026llm: broader languages and CWE classes [@li2026llm, p. 18] [A];
    - deininger2026open: other languages [@deininger2026open, p. 25] [A];
    - lu2025lab: VentiVul is C/C++ only and may not generalise to other languages [@lu2025lab, p. 17] [A].
## G6: No cost-per-confirmed-vulnerability comparison that includes human triage effort and a costed SAST and DL arm on the same targets
- Gap type: practical
- **Second-pass verdict: narrowed.** deininger2026open now reports compute cost (USD) and energy (kJ) per true positive at realistic prevalence for 8 LLMs. What remains open is (a) the human triage term, i.e. analyst time spent on the false positives that come with each true positive, and (b) a quan
- Evidence that the gap exists:
  - **Most studies report no monetary cost.** 13 of our 20 primary studies report none [I, our count]. The seven that do are du, guo, li2026llm, shu, tan, xiong and deininger [@du2026reducing, p. 8; @guo2025repoaudit, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 16; @shu2026evaluating, p. 42; @tan2026think, p. 10; @xiong20
  - **Where measured, cost is decisive.**
    - Per project: from $2.54 in the RepoAudit paper to $172.77 on average and $1,247.66 at most in li2026llm [@guo2025repoaudit, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 16] [V].
    - Thinking mode costs 2.7–4.4× the energy [@tan2026think, p. 10] [V]; in deininger2026open reasoning costs 4.5–12.1× more per task [@deininger2026open, p. 18] [V].
  - **Compute cost per true positive now exists for LLMs, but not for the other families and not for triage.**
    - deininger2026open reports USD 0.003 (Gemma-3-4B) to 0.212 (Claude-Sonnet-5) and 3.7 to 119.6 kJ per true positive at 1:44 prevalence [@deininger2026open, p. 8] [V].
    - Flawfinder is given as ≈0 cost per true positive [@deininger2026open, p. 8] [V]. No cost per true positive is quantified for CodeBERT ("negligible inference cost") or for Cppcheck and Semgrep [@deininger2026open, p. 8; @deininger2026open, p. 11] [V].
    - Each LLM true positive comes with 25.6–41.9 false positives [@deininger2026open, p. 8] [V]. The paper notes that no triage workflow absorbs that alert volume [@deininger2026open, p. 8] [A], but analyst time is not costed [I]. At such ratios analyst time would plausibly dominate compute cost of
    - Caveat for anyone reusing Table 5: its kJ per true positive for Qwen3-Coder-30B (4.0) and Llama-3.3-70B (44.8) uses FLOP estimates, not the measured per-task energy (88 J and 738 J) [@deininger2026open, p. 7; @deininger2026open, p. 8; @deininger2026open, p. 14] [V].
